complains of lethargy, fever and joint pain, particularly in both knees. He
has also noticed an intermittent rash on his arms and his neck. These

secondary to hypertension. His medication includes bisoprolol, aspirin
and hydralazine/isosorbide dinitrate.

complains of lethargy, fever and joint pain, particularly in both knees. He
has also noticed an intermittent rash on his arms and his neck. These
symptoms have progressed over the last six months. He has a past
medical history of congestive cardiac failure and chronic renal failure
secondary to hypertension. His medication includes bisoprolol, aspirin
and hydralazine/isosorbide dinitrate.
On examination the patient has no evidence of joint swelling. He has
discrete patches of scaling on his neck and forearms. He has normal
power in his arms and legs.
The following blood tests were obtained;

Positive
Anti-nuclear antibody
Positive

Positive
Anti-extractable nuclear Antigen
Negative
Anti-histone antibodies
Positve
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A polymorphous rash would expect to be erythematous and less
associated with systemic symptoms. Dermatomyositis may have a
positive ENA (anti-Jo1) with heliotrope rash and Gottrons papulses.
There also may be associated muscle weakness. Rheumatoid arthritis
would expect to show arthritis and is less associated with a rash and the
antibody picture. SLE is more associated with double stranded DNA and
ENA.
Drug induced lupus can be caused by a variety of drugs but most
commonly antihypertensives and antifungals. Specific examples include
isoniazid, hydralazine, procainamide, diltiazem and phenytoin. Anti-
histone antibodies are associated with drug-induced lupus in most
cases.
Drug-induced lupus
In drug-induced lupus not all the typical features of systemic lupus
erythematosus are seen, with renal and nervous system involvement
being unusual. It usually resolves on stopping the drug.

a four-week history of gastric reflux, which has not improved despite
being prescribed both ranitidine and omeprazole by her GP. She is
awaiting an urgent OGD to investigate symptoms further. She reports
having lost 7kg in weight over the past 6 months and is also distressed
by appearances of white hard lumps appearing on her fingertips. On
examination, you note cool peripheries and dry mucous membranes, left
thumb calcinosis surrounded by shiny skin up to her wrist joint and
wrinkling of skin around her mouth. Her blood tests are as follows
demonstrate she is positive for anticentromere antibodies. What is the
most likely diagnosis?
Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis
Systemic sclerosis sine scleroderma
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis

a four-week history of gastric reflux, which has not improved despite
being prescribed both ranitidine and omeprazole by her GP. She is
awaiting an urgent OGD to investigate symptoms further. She reports
having lost 7kg in weight over the past 6 months and is also distressed
by appearances of white hard lumps appearing on her fingertips. On
examination, you note cool peripheries and dry mucous membranes, left
thumb calcinosis surrounded by shiny skin up to her wrist joint and
wrinkling of skin around her mouth. Her blood tests are as follows
demonstrate she is positive for anticentromere antibodies. What is the
most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Systemic sclerosis (SS) is a fairly clear answer when presented with a
combination of sclerodactyly, calcinosis, perioral puckering and gastro-
oesophageal reflux symptoms in a middle-aged female. The main
differentials are whether this represents diffuse cutaneous, limited
cutaneous or systemic sclerosis sine scleroderma. The latter describes
patients with systemic involvement and possible Raynaud's
phenomenon in the absence of other cutaneous manifestations with
detection of SS autoantibodies. SS can be described generally as diffuse
when skin proximal to the distal forearm is involved, such as the elbow,
thorax or abdomen. Note that both limited and diffuse cutaneous SS has
extracutaneous involvement: however, patients with diffuse cutaneous
SS are more likely to develop significant renal, lung and cardiac disease.
Autoantibodies are useful in confirming the subtype of SS and predict
extracutaneous involvement but negative results do not rule out SS. Anti-
centromere antibodies are associated with limited cutaneous SS1, anti-
Scl 70 with diffuse SS and lung involvement , anti-RNA polymerase III to
those at high risk of scleroderma renal crisis , anti-U3-RNP to those at
high risk of pulmonary hypertension  and anti-PM-Scl to those at high
risk of SS associated myositis .
1. Reveille JD, Solomon DH et al. Evidence-based guidelines for the use
of immunologic tests: anticentromere, Scl-70, and nucleolar antibodies.
Arthritis Rheum. 2003;49(3):399
2. Nguyen B, Mayes MD, Arnett FC et al. HLA-DRB1*0407 and *1304 are
risk factors for scleroderma renal crisis. Arthritis Rheum.
2011;63(2):530.
3. Sacks DG, Okano Y, Steen VD et al. Isolated pulmonary hypertension in
systemic sclerosis with diffuse cutaneous involvement: association with
serum anti-U3RNP antibody. J Rheumatol. 1996;23(4):639
4. Oddis CV, Okano Y, Rudert WA et al. Serum autoantibody to the
nucleolar antigen PM-Scl. Clinical and immunogenetic associations.
Arthritis Rheum. 1992;35(10):1211

You see a 29-year-old patient with a swollen left knee. It has been getting
worse for a number of months and is now affecting his ability to work as
a postman. The pain and stiffness are worse overnight and in the
morning and gets better throughout the day. He denies any trauma or
fever. He also has some pain and stiffness in his fingers which is also
worse in the morning. His joints are worse after rest.
He is normally fit and well and denies any previous joint problems or
psoriasis. However, his father has a history of psoriasis. He says there is
no family history of joint problems to his knowledge.
On examination, his knee is red, warm and tender to palpate. There is a
moderate knee effusion and flexion is limited due to pain. His distal
interphalangeal joints (DIPs) are tender and slightly swollen.
There are no skin rashes. Although his knee is painful the patient looks
well and has a heart rate of 80 beats per minute and his temperature is
36.8ºC.
Blood tests reveal a raised CRP at 85 but a negative rheumatoid factor.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis
Psoriatic arthritis
Septic arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis

worse for a number of months and is now affecting his ability to work as
a postman. The pain and stiffness are worse overnight and in the
morning and gets better throughout the day. He denies any trauma or
fever. He also has some pain and stiffness in his fingers which is also
worse in the morning. His joints are worse after rest.
He is normally fit and well and denies any previous joint problems or
psoriasis. However, his father has a history of psoriasis. He says there is
no family history of joint problems to his knowledge.
On examination, his knee is red, warm and tender to palpate. There is a
moderate knee effusion and flexion is limited due to pain. His distal
interphalangeal joints (DIPs) are tender and slightly swollen.
There are no skin rashes. Although his knee is painful the patient looks
well and has a heart rate of 80 beats per minute and his temperature is
36.8ºC.
Blood tests reveal a raised CRP at 85 but a negative rheumatoid factor.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Given the inflammatory pattern of pain and swelling (worse in the
morning and after rest), the joints involved (DIPs and knee) and family
history of psoriasis, the most likely diagnosis is psoriatic arthritis.
Psoriatic arthropathy can present before psoriatic skin changes.
Therefore, option 3 is the correct answer.
Rheumatoid arthritis and seronegative rheumatoid arthritis classically
affect the metacarpal phalangeal joints (MCPs) of the hands, not the
DIPs. You would also expect the rheumatoid factor to be raised in
rheumatoid arthritis (but not seronegative rheumatoid arthritis).
Idiopathic juvenile arthritis presents like rheumatoid arthritis in patients
under 16 years old. Given the age of this patient, this is not a likely
diagnosis.
Septic arthritis presents with a swollen, red and very painful joint. The
patient would classically be pyrexial and unwell. Therefore, this is not the
most likely diagnosis.
Therefore, option 3 is the most likely diagnosis.
Psoriatic arthropathy
Psoriatic arthropathy is an inflammatory arthritis associated with
psoriasis and is classed as one of the seronegative
spondyloarthropathies. It correlates poorly with cutaneous psoriasis and
often precedes the development of skin lesions. Around 10-20% of
patients with skin lesions develop an arthropathy, with males and
Psoriatic arthropathy can present before psoriatic skin lesions - a
positive family history of psoriasis may point towards this diagnosis

A 54-year-old woman attends with worsening shortness of breath. She
has also complained of general arthralgia and severe fatigue. Her left
knee had previously been red and swollen but improved with an intra-
articular steroid injection. She notices around 10 minutes of early
morning stiffness and then has generalised joint pains throughout the
day that are worsened by over-exertion.
She has a past medical history of depression and Raynauds.
On examination, she has fine inspiratory crepitations in the lower zones.
She has a reduction in her range of movement when abducting her
shoulders with associated pain. The skin on her chest feels thickened.
She has white nodules around her right wrist and distal interphalangeal
joints.
Pulmonary function tests show:
FEV1 55% of predicted
FVC 65% of predicted
FEV1/FVC 0.85
DLCO 60% of predicted
Given the likely diagnosis, what is most likely to be raised in this patient?
ANCA
Anti-Scl-70 antibodies
Anti-centromere antibodies
Rheumatoid factor
Urate

has also complained of general arthralgia and severe fatigue. Her left
knee had previously been red and swollen but improved with an intra-

day that are worsened by over-exertion.
She has a past medical history of depression and Raynauds.
On examination, she has fine inspiratory crepitations in the lower zones.
She has a reduction in her range of movement when abducting her
shoulders with associated pain. The skin on her chest feels thickened.
She has white nodules around her right wrist and distal interphalangeal
joints.
Pulmonary function tests show:
FEV1 55% of predicted
FVC 65% of predicted
FEV1/FVC 0.85
DLCO 60% of predicted
Given the likely diagnosis, what is most likely to be raised in this patient?
explanation:
This patient has shortness of breath with fine crackles and a restrictive
pattern on lung function testing. She has scleroderma over her chest and
shoulders, as indicated by the thickened skin to palpate and reduction in
shoulder abduction. The white nodules on her wrist and fingers are likely
calcinosis. The most likely diagnosis here is diffuse cutaneous systemic
sclerosis.
Anti-scl-70 antibodies is correct. Anti-scl-70 antibodies are associated
with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis. The pattern of disease here -
truncal scleroderma, respiratory involvement - is the classical findings in
diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis rather than the limited type. The
anti-scl-70 antibodies are associated with a higher risk of severe lung
disease.
Anti-centromere antibodies is incorrect. Anti-centromere antibodies are
associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. The pattern of
disease here - truncal scleroderma, respiratory involvement - is the
classical findings in diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis rather than the
limited type.
Rheumatoid factor is incorrect. Although 30% of patients diagnosed with
systemic sclerosis are rheumatoid factor positive, this patient likely has
diffuse cutaneous sclerosis (given the truncal thickened skin and lung
involvement). Studies have shown that up to 70% of patients with diffuse
systemic sclerosis will have positive anti-scl-70 antibodies, this is,
therefore, the better answer. Rheumatoid factor can also be associated
with rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis wouldn't explain the skin
changes over her chest and shoulders, and it is less common for
rheumatoid arthritis to present with monoarticular large joint effusion
and exertional pain. You would expect to see an asymmetrical
polyarthritis particularly in the small joints of the hands, with morning
stiffness and improvement once 'getting going'.
ANCA is incorrect. ANCA positivity is seen in multiple autoimmune
conditions, particularly vasculitis. Although this patient has some
arthralgia and previous joint swelling, her other symptoms are not
Anti-scl-70 antibodies are associated with a higher risk of severe
interstitial lung disease in systemic sclerosis
particularly suggestive of vasculitis. ANCA vasculitis can rarely lead to
pulmonary vasculitis via progressive small-volume alveolar haemorrhage
and scarring caused directly by anti-MPO antibodies, but this is unusual.
Urate is incorrect. Although they can appear similar, the white lesions
described would be more in keeping with calcinosis than gouty tophi
given the rest of the clinical picture. Gout would not explain the
restrictive lung pictures or skin changes across her chest.
Systemic sclerosis

hardened, sclerotic skin and other connective tissues. It is four times
more common in females.

Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis

scleroderma affects face and distal limbs predominately
associated with anti-centromere antibodies
a subtype of limited systemic sclerosis is CREST syndrome:
Calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, oEsophageal dysmotility,
Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia
Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis
scleroderma affects trunk and proximal limbs predominately
associated with anti scl-70 antibodies
the most common cause of death is now respiratory involvement,
which is seen in around 80%: interstitial lung disease (ILD) and

A 68-year-old woman presents to a care of the elderly clinic. This is her
first attendance following recent frequent falls at home. Her most recent
fall was two weeks ago during which time she had a CT head/c-
spine/right hip which was negative for any acute injury.
Her only symptom between falls is a pain in her right hip which has been
worsening over the past year. This is worse on activity and in the
evenings. She is tender to deep palpation and has painful internal and
external rotation on examination. Otherwise, she reports that she is well
in herself and her only past medical history includes obesity and type 2
diabetes mellitus. She has been advised by her general practitioner to
lose weight.
Which of the following is the most appropriate additional advice for her
hip pain?
Elevate lower limbs when seated
Muscle strengthening exercises and aerobic fitness
Reduce alcohol intake
Regular rest throughout the day
Smoking cessation

A 68-year-old woman presents to a care of the elderly clinic. This is her
first attendance following recent frequent falls at home. Her most recent
fall was two weeks ago during which time she had a CT head/c-
spine/right hip which was negative for any acute injury.
Her only symptom between falls is a pain in her right hip which has been
worsening over the past year. This is worse on activity and in the
evenings. She is tender to deep palpation and has painful internal and
external rotation on examination. Otherwise, she reports that she is well
in herself and her only past medical history includes obesity and type 2
diabetes mellitus. She has been advised by her general practitioner to
lose weight.
Which of the following is the most appropriate additional advice for her
hip pain?
options: Muscle strengthening exercises and aerobic fitness
explanation:
This woman has osteoarthritis of the right hip. This is evidenced by the
chronicity and nature of the pain. These factors, as well as her recent
negative imaging, make acute injury unlikely. As per the latest NICE
Local muscle strengthening exercises and general aerobic fitness is
an important component of knee and hip osteoarthritis
guidance, all patients diagnosed with osteoarthritis of the knee or hip
should be offered help with weight loss, given advice about local muscle
strengthening exercises and general aerobic fitness.
Elevating limbs is helpful in acute injury to reduce acute swelling but will
not affect this woman's osteoarthritis.
Reducing alcohol intake is a preventative measure for gout however
would not be effective in this case.
Regular rest throughout the day may temporarily prevent symptoms but
will be debilitating and not result in any lasting improvement.
Smoking cessation is useful in rheumatoid arthritis however the history
here is more classical of osteoarthritis.

stem: A 24-year-old man of Armenian descent presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, fever, and joint pain. He reports having similar episodes since childhood, each lasting 2-3 days before resolving spontaneously. His maternal uncle and cousin have similar symptoms. During an attack, he develops a painful rash on his lower legs. Physical examination reveals diffuse abdominal tenderness with guarding and a temperature of 39.2°C. Blood tests show an elevated white cell count and C-reactive protein. Between episodes, he is completely well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Familial Mediterranean fever
Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is an autosomal recessive, hereditary inflammatory disorder characterised by reoccurring episodes of abdominal pain, fever, arthralgia, and chest pain. This patient presents with classic features of FMF including recurrent episodes of fever, severe abdominal pain due to peritonitis, and joint pain that last 2-3 days before resolving completely. The patient's Armenian ethnicity is significant as FMF is particularly common in populations from the Mediterranean basin, including Turkish, Armenian, Arab, and Sephardic Jewish populations. The family history suggests an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, which is typical of FMF. The painful rash on the lower legs is likely erysipeloid rash, a characteristic finding in FMF. The elevated inflammatory markers during attacks with complete resolution between episodes is also consistent with this diagnosis. FMF is caused by mutations in the MEFV gene, which encodes pyrin, a protein involved in regulating inflammation. Treatment typically involves daily colchicine, which can prevent attacks and reduce the risk of amyloidosis, a serious long-term complication.

Behçet's disease
Behçet's disease is incorrect. While Behçet's disease can also present with recurrent episodes of inflammation and is more common in populations from the Mediterranean and Middle East, its hallmark features include recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis, and various skin lesions. The patient's presentation lacks these characteristic features, particularly the absence of oral and genital ulceration makes Behçet's disease unlikely.

Inflammatory bowel disease
Inflammatory bowel disease is incorrect. While IBD can present with abdominal pain, fever, and extraintestinal manifestations including joint pain and skin lesions, the episodic nature with complete resolution between attacks is less typical. Additionally, IBD would typically present with more persistent gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhoea, rectal bleeding, or weight loss, which are not mentioned in this case. The family history pattern is also not consistent with IBD.

Hereditary angioedema
Hereditary angioedema is incorrect. This condition is characterized by recurrent episodes of severe swelling affecting the skin, gastrointestinal tract, and upper airways. While abdominal pain can occur due to intestinal wall oedema, the presentation typically lacks fever and joint pain. Additionally, hereditary angioedema follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, which doesn't align with the family history described in this case.

Adult-onset Still's disease
Adult-onset Still's disease is incorrect. While this condition can present with high fevers, joint pain, and a characteristic salmon-pink rash, it typically has a more persistent course rather than discrete episodes with complete resolution. The rash in Still's disease is typically evanescent and appears during fever spikes, unlike the lower leg rash described in this case. Additionally, Still's disease is not known to have a strong genetic component or ethnic predisposition as described in this scenario.

systemic lupus erythematosus. While SLE can cause pericarditis,
arthritis, fever and in rare cases, peritonitis, the antinuclear antibody is
negative, making this diagnosis very unlikely.
Prednisolone is incorrect. This can be used to treat protracted febrile
myalgia in FMF but is not first-line therapy.
Colchicine may be helpful in Familial Mediterranean Fever

stem: A 24-year-old male comes into the GP with due to constant bruising. On examination, he has an early-diastolic murmur over the aortic region. His skin is very elastic and his joints extend further than they normally should. He is referred for genetic tests, which confirm the suspected diagnosis of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Which type of collagen is primarily affected by Ehlers-Danlos syndrome?
explanation:
Collagen type 3
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is most commonly associated with a defect in type III collagen. Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is primarily caused by a genetic defect in collagen type III.

Collagen type 1
Collagen type I is defective in osteogenesis imperfecta.

Collagen type 4
Collagen IV is defective in Goodpasture's syndrome.

Collagen type 5
Collagen Type V is affected in a less common variant of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents to her GP with a 6-month history of joint pain and stiffness, especially in her wrists and small joints of her hands. She reports morning stiffness lasting over an hour and persistent fatigue. On examination, her joints are swollen, warm, and tender. This is evidence of hyperextension of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints and flexion of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints. X-rays show joint space narrowing and early erosions in the hand joints. What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
explanation:
Methotrexate with short-term bridging corticosteroids
Methotrexate with short-term bridging corticosteroids represents the correct initial management approach. Methotrexate is the first-line DMARD for RA, aiming to slow disease progression and prevent joint damage, while corticosteroids provide immediate symptomatic relief during the period required for methotrexate to exert its full effect.

Infliximab with NSAIDs
Infliximab with NSAIDs is not typically utilised as first-line therapy in RA. These agents are generally reserved for patients with an inadequate response to at least two conventional DMARDs including methotrexate or those presenting with severe disease activity.

Corticosteroids with NSAIDs
Corticosteroids with NSAIDs are not recommended for long-term management of RA. Although they effectively reduce inflammation and control symptoms rapidly, their use is usually limited to short-term relief —often serving as 'bridging' therapy while awaiting the onset of action from DMARDs such as methotrexate. Long-term corticosteroid use carries significant risks including osteoporosis, weight gain, and increased susceptibility to infections; furthermore, chronic concurrent administration of corticosteroids and NSAIDs heightens the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding among other complications.

Hydroxychloroquine monotherapy
Hydroxychloroquine is indeed a DMARD employed in treating RA; however, it typically does not suffice as monotherapy for initial management. It may be used concomitantly with other DMARDs like methotrexate in more severe cases or when milder forms of RA are being treated. Hydroxychloroquine can serve as an adjunctive treatment but for initial management purposes, a combination of methotrexate and short-term corticosteroids is preferred due to their ability to more swiftly control inflammation and prevent joint damage.

NSAIDs with paracetamol
NSAIDs with paracetamol do not represent optimal initial management for a patient presenting with RA. While NSAIDs and paracetamol may alleviate pain and inflammation symptoms, they fail to modify the underlying disease process or forestall joint destruction. Initial treatment protocols typically involve DMARDs such as methotrexate that aim to retard disease progression and mitigate long-term articular damage. NSAIDs and paracetamol might be utilised adjunctively but are insufficient on their own as comprehensive treatment strategies for effectively managing RA.

stem: Which one of the following statements regarding raloxifene in the management of osteoporosis is incorrect?
options: Has been shown to prevent bone loss and to reduce the risk of vertebral fractures
Is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator
Increases the risk of breast cancer
explanation:
Increases the risk of breast cancer
The correct answer is 'Increases the risk of breast cancer'. Raloxifene, a selective oestrogen receptor modulator (SERM), has been shown to reduce the risk of invasive breast cancer in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and in postmenopausal women at high risk for invasive breast cancer. It achieves this by blocking the effects of oestrogen on breast tissue.

Has been shown to prevent bone loss and to reduce the risk of vertebral fractures
Has been shown to prevent bone loss and to reduce the risk of vertebral fractures' is indeed a correct statement about raloxifene. This drug works by mimicking the effects of oestrogen on bone tissue, thereby reducing bone resorption and turnover, ultimately leading to increased bone mineral density and reduced incidence of fractures.

Is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator
Is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator' is also accurate. Raloxifene belongs to a class of drugs known as SERMs. They selectively bind to oestrogen receptors in different tissues, acting as agonists or antagonists depending on the specific tissue. In bone tissue, raloxifene acts as an oestrogen agonist, hence its utility in managing osteoporosis.

May worsen menopausal symptoms
May worsen menopausal symptoms' is another true statement about raloxifene. While it mimics the beneficial effects of oestrogen on bones, it does not have the same effect on other tissues where oestrogen has a role, such as those involved in maintaining temperature regulation. Therefore, it may exacerbate hot flushes and other menopausal symptoms.

Increases risk of thromboembolic events
Increases risk of thromboembolic events' is also true about raloxifene. Similar to hormone replacement therapy (HRT), raloxifene increases the risk of venous thromboembolism including deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Therefore, it should be used with caution in patients with risk factors for these conditions.

stem: A 27-year-old man is referred to the rheumatology team due to worsening back pain and stiffness. After investigations, including blood tests and a spine X-ray, the patient is diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis. Initial treatments include naproxen and etoricoxib. His symptoms are refractory to these treatments, and so, after discussing at the multidisciplinary team meeting, a trial of golimumab is agreed upon. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
explanation:
Tumour necrosis factor alpha antagonist
Golimumab is a TNF inhibitor. The correct answer is tumour necrosis factor (TNF) alpha antagonist. Golimumab is one of several TNF inhibitors approved for the treatment of refractory ankylosing spondylitis. It is administered subcutaneously every 4 weeks.

CD20 antagonist
An example of a CD20 antagonist is rituximab. This is used in the management of rheumatoid arthritis as well as several haematological malignancies.

CD38 antagonist
CD38 antagonists include drugs such as daratumumab, with others in various stages of clinical trials. Daratumumab is licensed (under specialist use) for the treatment of multiple myeloma.

Interleukin-1 inhibitor
Interleukin-1 inhibitors include anakinra, which differs from the natural 'interleukin-1 receptor antagonist' by just one amino acid. It is used in the management of rheumatoid arthritis.

Interleukin-17A inhibitor
Interleukin-17A inhibitors include secukinumab. Under specialist use, this is also licensed for the treatment of ankylosing spondylitis.

stem: Which one of the following is least recognised as a risk factor for developing osteoporosis?
explanation:
Hypothyroidism
The correct answer is Hypothyroidism. Whilst hypothyroidism can affect bone metabolism, it is not as strongly associated with osteoporosis as the other conditions listed. In fact, the relationship between hypothyroidism and bone mineral density is complex, and studies have shown conflicting results. Some research suggests that adequately treated hypothyroidism has minimal impact on bone health.

Cushing's syndrome
Cushing's syndrome is a well-established risk factor for osteoporosis. The excess glucocorticoids in Cushing's syndrome directly inhibit osteoblast function and enhance osteoclast activity, leading to decreased bone formation and increased bone resorption. Additionally, glucocorticoids interfere with calcium absorption in the gut and increase urinary calcium excretion.

Turner's syndrome
Turner's syndrome is strongly associated with osteoporosis due to oestrogen deficiency and other genetic factors. The absence of the second X chromosome results in accelerated bone loss and reduced peak bone mass. These patients typically require early oestrogen replacement therapy to optimise bone health.

Hyperparathyroidism
Hyperparathyroidism causes significant bone loss through increased osteoclast activity. The excess parathyroid hormone leads to enhanced bone resorption, mobilising calcium from the skeleton. This results in reduced bone mineral density, particularly affecting cortical bone, and increases fracture risk.

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus, both type 1 and type 2, is associated with increased fracture risk and osteoporosis. Type 1 diabetes affects peak bone mass acquisition, while type 2 diabetes affects bone quality through advanced glycation end-products and altered bone turnover. The combination of metabolic derangements and increased fall risk makes diabetes a significant risk factor for osteoporotic fractures.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is referred to the Medical Admissions Unit with a 3-day history of weakness in her left foot and right wrist. She has also lost 5kg of weight over the previous three weeks. She has no past medical history and does not take any regular medications. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. Her observations are as follows: Heart rate of 88 beats per minute Blood pressure of 145/92 mmHg Respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min Temperature of 37.2ºC Oxygen saturation of 96% on room air On examination, there is weakness of left foot dorsiflexion and right wrist extension. There is no evidence of cervical, inguinal or axillary lymphadenopathy. There is a rash suggestive of livedo reticularis on her lower limbs. The examination is otherwise unremarkable. Blood tests: Hb 123 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 444 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 7.2 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Na+ 137 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 8.2 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 101 µmol/L (55 - 120) CRP 54 mg/L (< 5) ESR 101 mm/hr (<20) Bilirubin 14 µmol/L (3 - 17) ALP 89 u/L (30 - 100) ALT 44 u/L (3 - 40) Î³GT 62 u/L (8 - 60) Albumin 35 g/L (35 - 50) Further testing: Anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibody (ANCA) negative Antinuclear antibody (ANA) negative Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) positive Urinalysis: Blood ++ Protein + Leucocytes -ve Nitrites -ve Plain radiography of the chest is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polyarteritis nodosa
Polyarteritis nodosa can cause a mononeuritis multiplex syndrome. The patient presents with weight loss, mononeuritis multiplex, hypertension, haematuria, proteinuria and livedo reticularis with serological evidence of hepatitis B infection. These features are consistent with a diagnosis of polyarteritis nodosa, which is associated with infection with hepatitis B.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is incorrect. This can cause mononeuritis multiplex, haematuria, proteinuria, livedo reticularis and raised inflammatory markers but the ANCA being negative makes this less likely. Furthermore, there is not a classic association with hepatitis B, compared with PAN.

Kawasaki disease
Kawasaki disease is incorrect. This is another medium vessel vasculitis that can cause a mononeuritis multiplex. However, it is typically associated with children and the development of coronary artery aneurysms.

Lymphoma
Lymphoma is incorrect. This can cause a mononeuritis-type picture but the absence of cytopenias and lymphadenopathy make this less likely.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus is incorrect. This can cause mononeuritis and livedo reticularis. However, the negative anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) test makes this very unlikely.

stem: A 57-year-old man presents to his GP with right-sided hip stiffness and difficulty mobilising. He reports no history of trauma. Although he has no significant past medical history, he discloses that he has been consuming approximately 750ml of vodka daily for the past 10 years. On examination, there is pain and a reduced range of movement in all directions of the right hip, while the left side remains unaffected. What is the best imaging modality to confirm the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
MRI
MRI is the investigation of choice for avascular necrosis of the hip. The patient has presented with unilateral right-sided hip pain and restricted movement. When considered alongside the patient's history of chronic alcohol abuse, these symptoms are highly indicative of avascular necrosis of the hip. MRI is recognised as the superior imaging technique for establishing a diagnosis of avascular necrosis of the hip.

CT
CT scans are not routinely employed to diagnose avascular necrosis of the hip due to their inferior accuracy when compared to MRI. Although CT can provide more intricate images of complex fractures that may be useful pre-operatively, there is no reported trauma in this case to suggest that a fracture has occurred.

Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA)
DEXA scanning is instrumental in measuring bone mineral density and diagnosing conditions such as osteopenia and osteoporosis, but it is not utilised for detecting avascular necrosis of the hip, which remains our primary concern in this scenario.

Radionuclide bone scan
Radionuclide bone scans require administering a small quantity of radioactive isotope that emits gamma rays detectable through analysis. This isotopic uptake occurs at specific sites, including malignancies; however, such scans are not routinely conducted for avascular necrosis of the hip since MRI has proven more sensitive for diagnostic purposes.

X-ray
An X-ray might typically be ordered initially but often yields normal results, particularly in early disease stages. An MRI's greater sensitivity makes it the preferred imaging modality under these circumstances.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with pain in the left knee of several months' duration. It is stiff for 10 to 15 minutes in the morning and generally affects her ability to walk and perform her daily activities. Her past medical history includes hypertension, for which she takes amlodipine. On examination, there is no obvious swelling or deformity of the left knee. Movement is generally restricted due to pain. Observations are all within normal limits. What is the most appropriate first step in management?
explanation:
Topical ibuprofen
Knee osteoarthritis - topical NSAIDs are first-line. This patient's presentation is suggestive of knee osteoarthritis, given her age, gradual onset of pain, functional limitation and lack of significant morning stiffness. NICE guidelines regarding osteoarthritis were updated in 2022 and no longer advocate the use of paracetamol or weak opioids unless they are used infrequently and for short-term relief. First-line management for the knee is the use of topical NSAIDs such as topical ibuprofen.

Intra-articular steroid injection
Intra-articular steroid injection is incorrect. This may be offered if initial pharmacotherapy is not effective. However, patients should be warned of the limited duration of efficacy and the potential for side effects.

Oral codeine
Oral codeine is incorrect. Weak opioids should not be offered first-line, and should only be used if NSAIDs have been unsuccessful or are unsuitable.

Oral dihydrocodeine
Oral dihydrocodeine is incorrect. As with oral codeine, this is a weak opioid and should not be used first-line.

Oral ibuprofen
Oral ibuprofen is incorrect. Oral NSAIDs carry a higher risk of side effects given their systemic effect, including renal impairment and gastric irritation. They may be used if topical NSAIDs are insufficient - however, the latter should be tried first-line.

stem: A 67-year-old woman who is taking long-term prednisolone for polymyalgia rheumatica presents with progressive pain in her right hip joint. A diagnosis of avascular necrosis is suspected. Which investigation is most likely to be diagnostic?
explanation:
MRI
MRI is therefore the investigation of choice.

Radionuclide bone scan
In early avascular necrosis a radionuclide bone scan is less sensitive than MRI and the findings may be nonspecific.

stem: A 33-year-old man presents to his GP with joint pains. He describes pains in his legs and hips, but his biggest concern is back pain. He finds he is very stiff in the morning, but this improves with exercise. The GP considers investigations for ankylosing spondylitis. What feature would most support this diagnosis?
options: Loss of joint space on x-ray
Presence of anticyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies
explanation:
Sacro-ilitis on pelvic x-ray
Diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis can be best supported by sacroilitis on a pelvic X-ray. This is a finding suggestive of ankylosing spondylitis. Other radiographic features would include erosions, sclerosis, vertebral syndesmophytes and calcification of ligaments.

Atlanto-axial instability
Atlanto-axial instability can be seen in rheumatoid arthritis but is not suggestive of ankylosing spondylitis.

Loss of joint space on x-ray
This is associated with rheumatoid arthritis and is not seen in ankylosing spondylitis.

Positive HLA-B27
HLA-B27 is not a diagnostic test for ankylosing spondylitis. It is present in approximately 90% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis but is also present in about 8% of the general population, most of whom do not have ankylosing spondylitis.

Presence of anticyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies
Anticyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies are highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis, not ankylosing spondylitis.

stem: A 28-year-old female is referred to the medical assessment unit by her general practitioner with reports of a three-week history of rash and joint pains. She has no past medical history and does not take any regular medications. On examination, there is a butterfly-shaped rash over her cheeks and nose that spares the nasolabial folds. The small joints of her hands are swollen and tender. Blood tests: Hb 136 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 101 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 2.3 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Na+ 137 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 5.2 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 88 µmol/L (55 - 120) CRP 4 mg/L (< 5) Antinuclear antibody positive (1:320) (negative) Which of the following medications should all patients with this condition be taking long term?
explanation:
Hydroxychloroquine
Hydroxychloroquine is the treatment of choice for SLE. Hydroxychloroquine is considered to be the 'anchor drug' for long term maintenance therapy of SLE and all patients should be commenced on this treatment at diagnosis.

Azathioprine
Azathioprine is incorrect. This can be used as a steroid-sparing agent in SLE. However, it is only indicated in diseases of at least moderate severity where initial measures have not been successful. Typical examples of disease features of moderate severity include fever, pleurisy, pericarditis or severe cutaneous vasculitis. Every patient with SLE will not need this medication.

Belimumab
Belimumab is incorrect. This is a fully-humanized IgG1Î³ monoclonal antibody directed against a soluble B lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS). It is principally used as an additional therapy in patients with the active autoantibody-positive disease who are already receiving therapy with conventional immunosuppression. It is typically used for skin and musculoskeletal manifestations of the disease. It will therefore not be indicated in all patients.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone is incorrect. Patients with SLE may need prednisolone to induce remission and in some cases, may find it difficult to wean prednisolone and will need to be on a small maintenance dose. However, this is not an ideal situation and the aim is for steroid-free management of the disease.

Rituximab
Rituximab is incorrect. This is used for cases of SLE with life-threatening clinical manifestations e.g. renal/neuropsychiatric or those refractory to initial immunosuppression.

stem: A 28-year-old male with pseudoxanthoma elasticum attends the outpatient clinic for follow up. He has a family history of coronary artery disease and is concerned about his risk. A routine echo is done as part of his cardiovascular evaluation. What is the most common finding on echocardiography in these patients?
explanation:
Mitral valve prolapse
Pseudoxanthoma elasticum is associated with mitral valve prolapse and increased risk of ischaemic heart disease. In pseudoxanthoma elasticum, cardiovascular abnormalities are common. General cardiovascular abnormalities such as hypertension and peripheral vascular disease are common. It is also a cause for ischaemic heart disease in the young, due to progressive narrowing of small to medium-sized arteries due to elastorrhexis and calcification of elastic fibres in the vessel walls. Echocardiography is commonly done to monitor for any cardiac complications. The most common heart valve abnormality is mitral valve prolapse. It can occur in up to 70% of patients with pseudoxanthoma elasticum. It would show up clinically as a systolic murmur with a mid systolic click, accentuated by the Valsalva manoeuvre.

Aortic regurgitation
Aortic regurgitation has been documented but is far less common.

Thoracic aortic aneurysm
Aortic aneurysms are seen in patients with genetic abnormalities of blood vessels. Again, this is less common than mitral valve prolapse.

Dilated cardiomyopathy
Dilated cardiomyopathy is not often seen here and pseudoxanthoma elasticum is more associated with diastolic heart failure and restrictive cardiomyopathy.

Pulmonary hypertension
Pulmonary hypertension again is seen with narrowing of vasculature but is less common than mitral valve prolapse.

stem: A 60-year-old man with worsening dyspnoea was seen in the emergency department. His past medical history included diabetes mellitus. Additionally, a number of years before this, he had seen a dermatologist for intermittent erythema and swelling in the right auricle and nasal deformity, but no conclusive diagnosis was made. He had intermittent breathing difficulties for the past year, which was getting worse. What is the overarching diagnosis in this case?
options: Mouth and genital ulcers with inflamed cartilage (MAGIC) syndrome
explanation:
Relapsing polychondritis
As well as ear problems, relapsing polychondritis may present with nasal chondritis, respiratory tract involvement and arthralgia. Relapsing polychondritis is a rare autoimmune disorder characterised by recurrent episodes of inflammation and destruction of cartilaginous tissues resulting in widespread chondritis of the auricular, nasal, and tracheal cartilages as described in this case. Clinical features can include recurrent chondritis of the laryngotracheobronchitis tree and potentially end up with life-threatening laryngotracheal stenosis.

Bronchiolitis obliterans
Bronchiolitis obliterans is incorrect as it is an inflammatory condition that affects the lung's tiniest airways, the bronchioles. Symptoms commonly include shortness of breath, dry cough and sometimes wheezing and fatigue in the absence of a cold or asthma. In affected people, the bronchioles may become damaged and inflamed leading to extensive scarring that blocks the airway.

Churg-Strauss syndrome
Churg-Strauss' syndrome, also known as allergic granulomatous angiitis, is a rare disease characterised by the triad of asthma, pulmonary infiltrates, and eosinophilia - rarely causing nasal chondritis or arthritis. Churg-Strauss syndrome is characterised by the presence of nasal polyps with a great tendency for relapse but does not cause nasal deformity or cartilage involvement, meaning this diagnosis is unlikely.

Leprosy
Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous infection of the skin and peripheral nerves that often leads to gross deformation of the nasal skeleton and subsequent formation of a saddle-nose deformity. However, the absence of hypopigmented patches and thickened peripheral nerves with some degree of sensory loss makes this diagnosis less likely.

Mouth and genital ulcers with inflamed cartilage (MAGIC) syndrome
Mouth and genital ulcers with inflamed cartilage (MAGIC) syndrome refer to a condition in which features of Behcet's disease and relapsing polychondritis occur in the same individual. The absence of mouth and genital ulcers makes this diagnosis incorrect here.

stem: A 64-year-old female presents with difficulty brushing her hair and standing up after sitting in her chair. There is a purple heliotropic rash above both eyes and a symmetrical erythematous papular rash over both hands. Blood tests identify a CK of 9543 and anti-nuclear antibody testing is positive. You make a diagnosis of dermatomyositis and initiate treatment with steroids. What is the most important next step?
options: Arrange CK to be re-checked by GP in 3 months
explanation:
Urgent malignancy screen
In patients with a new diagnosis of dermatomyositis, urgent malignancy screen is needed. Almost a quarter of individuals diagnosed with dermatomyositis have an underlying malignancy (typically ovarian, breast and lung cancer), this prevalence increases in the elderly.

Arrange CK to be re-checked by GP in 3 months
Serial CK measurement can be part of monitoring response to treatment but is not the most important next step.

HLA testing
HLA testing is not part of the workup for dermatomyositis.

Troponin I (high sensitivity)
Screening for cardiac involvement may be undertaken in idiopathic inflammatory myopathies but is not the most important next step.

VTE prophylaxis
VTE prophylaxis is not indicated.

stem: A 33-year-old woman has attended the rheumatology clinic with a 4-month history of symptoms. She describes her symptoms as starting as Raynaud's phenomenon, before progressing to arthralgia and myalgia. On further questioning, she describes oesophageal dysfunction and increasing dyspnoea. On clinical examination, there is evidence of dactylitis and a photosensitive rash affecting the chest and neck. There is no evidence of active synovitis. Blood tests are below. ANA Positive Anti-U1RNP Positive Anti-centromere Negative Anti-dsDNA Negative Anti-Scl70 Negative What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Mixed connective tissue disease
Anti-ribonuclear protein (anti-RNP) = mixed connective tissue disease. This scenario describes a young female with symptoms consistent with a multisystem disorder. The patient has an initial symptom of Raynaud's with subsequent development of dyspnoea, oesophageal dysmotility, photosensitive rash, and dactylitis. When these symptoms are combined with a positive anti-U1RNP, the diagnosis of mixed connective tissue disease can be made. Mixed connective tissue disease is a multisystem rheumatological disorder typically affecting females between 30 and 40 years of age. Raynaud's phenomenon is the initial symptom in 90% of cases and patients can have a multitude of symptoms and signs. Usually, antinuclear antibodies are positive and anti-U1RNP must be positive for a diagnosis to be made. Anti-U1RNP can be seen in other disorders such as systemic sclerosis and systemic lupus erythematosus, and so antibodies for these conditions, anti-centromere and anti-Scl70 along with anti-dsDNA, respectively, must be negative.

Anti-synthetase syndrome
Anti-synthetase syndrome is another multisystem disorder that typically presents with a triad of interstitial lung disease, inflammatory arthritis, and inflammatory myositis. Antibodies against tRNA synthetase are present, however, there are multiple that have been identified. Each antibody can cause a variety of different symptoms and signs. The most common are anti-Jo1, anti-PL7, and anti-PL12.

Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis
Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis is associated with anti-Scl70 and involves multi-organ dysfunction along with proximal skin thickening. Patients can develop interstitial lung disease and Raynaud's phenomenon along with cardiac, renal, and gastrointestinal fibrosis.

Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis
Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis is the other form of systemic sclerosis and is associated with anti-centromere. Patients typically develop Raynaud's disease before the onset of distal skin thickening. Telangiectasia is common and pulmonary arterial hypertension can occur.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), again, is a multisystem disorder. Patients can develop a malar rash, oral ulcers, pulmonary disease (including pulmonary haemorrhage, pleuritis, and pneumonitis), cardiac disease (including pericarditis and endocarditis) along with myalgia and arthralgia. SLE is associated with positive anti-dsDNA.

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents to her GP with several months of pain and stiffness in both knees and the hands. She also describes some swelling of the left index finger. She is otherwise well, with no significant past medical history except for hypertension, for which she takes amlodipine, and a cough which is currently under investigation. On examination, she has dactylitis of the left index finger, as well as generalised pain and poor mobility of the fingers. X-rays of the hands are taken: Hand X-rays Distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint erosions bilaterally. Which diagnosis would be most typical of the findings?
explanation:
Psoriatic arthritis
The diagnosis here is that of psoriatic arthritis. The correlation between this and cutaneous psoriasis is actually quite poor and arthritic symptoms often precede skin lesions. There is significant overlap with rheumatoid arthritis in terms of presentation, but the features of DIP joint disease and dactylitis point much more towards psoriatic arthritis rather than rheumatoid.

Gout
Gout is incorrect - this would be more acute and monoarticular or oligoarticular. It would not present with the other symptoms seen here.

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is incorrect. This would more commonly present asymmetrically, of a larger joint, and not have features such as dactylitis present, nor the findings on X-ray.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. Whilst some degree of overlap, as described above, DIP joint disease would be less likely, as well as dactylitis. A blood test should be undertaken to look for anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (anti-CCP) as these have a very high degree of specificity for rheumatoid arthritis, and are usually absent in psoriatic arthritis.

Sarcoid dactylitis
Sarcoid dactylitis is incorrect. Dactylitis is found in some patients with chronic sarcoid, but would not present with this patient's X-ray findings, and the patient would have other features of sarcoidosis. A cough is mentioned in the history as a red herring but this would not explain the other symptoms and X-ray findings in this scenario, and so psoriatic arthritis is still far more likely.

stem: A 66-year-old woman attends the clinic with weakness and muscle pain. On examination, you note a proximal muscle weakness of the upper (MRC grade 4/5) and lower (MRC grade 3/5) limbs. You also note a bilateral lilac discolouration of the eyelids with swelling of the eyelids and skin around the eyes. What antibody is most specific to the underlying condition?
explanation:
Anti-Jo-1 antibody
Dermatomyositis is associated with the anti-Jo-1 antibody. The patient most likely has a diagnosis of dermatomyositis as indicated by the proximal muscle weakness and heliotrope rash. Polymyositis and dermatomyositis are autoimmune disorders where there is inflammation in the muscles (myositis). Polymyositis is a condition of chronic inflammation of muscles. Dermatomyositis is a connective tissue disorder where there is a chronic inflammation of the skin and muscles. The presence of cutaneous manifestations, in this case, favours a diagnosis of dermatomyositis. Anti-Jo-1 antibody is correct. Although this antibody is not particularly sensitive to dermatomyositis, it is highly specific, making this the best answer. Antibodies to Jo1 are found in 20-60% of patients with primary polymyositis or dermatomyositis and less commonly in association with other connective tissue disease. Anti-Jo1 positive patients tend to have the poorest prognosis with more prominent lung involvement and less skin involvement.

Anti dsDNA antibody
Anti dsDNA is incorrect. The anti-double stranded DNA antibodies (anti-dsDNA) are considered a specific marker for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Although muscle weakness can occur in SLE, the presence of the heliotrope rash favours a diagnosis of dermatomyositis. Furthermore, the absence of other diagnostic criteria of SLE (e.g. oral ulcers, fever, and neurological dysfunction) makes it a less likely diagnosis.

Anti-PL-7 antibody
Anti-PL-7 antibody is incorrect. Although this can be positive in dermatomyositis, it is not sensitive nor specific to this condition.

Anti-Smith antibody
Anti-Smith is incorrect. Anti-Smith antibody is another highly specific antibody for SLE.

Antinuclear antibody
Antinuclear antibody (ANA) is incorrect. Although ANA is a relatively sensitive test, with the majority of patients (around 80%) being positive, it is not specific to dermatomyositis.

stem: A 40-year-old woman who is known to have systemic lupus erythematosus is reviewed with an exacerbation of wrist pain. Which one of the following is the most useful marker for monitoring disease activity?
explanation:
Anti-dsDNA titres
The correct answer is Anti-dsDNA titres. Anti-double stranded DNA (dsDNA) antibodies are highly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), and their levels correlate well with disease activity. They are present in up to 70% of patients with SLE, and their presence can be associated with renal involvement. Therefore, monitoring anti-dsDNA titres is useful in assessing disease activity and potential organ damage.

C-reactive protein
C-reactive protein (CRP) is an acute-phase reactant produced by the liver in response to inflammation. While it may be elevated during a flare of SLE, it's not specific for SLE and can be raised in many different conditions such as infection or other inflammatory diseases. Therefore, while CRP could indicate a flare, its utility as a marker for monitoring disease activity in SLE is limited compared to anti-dsDNA.

C2 levels
C2 levels refer to complement component 2, part of the immune system that enhances the ability of antibodies and phagocytic cells to clear microbes and damaged cells. Low C2 levels can occur in active SLE due to consumption by immune complexes but they do not correlate well with disease activity making them less useful as a marker.

Anti-nuclear antibody titres
Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) titres are often positive in patients with SLE given that it's an autoimmune condition where the body's immune system attacks its own tissues and organs. However, ANA positivity can also occur in healthy individuals or those with other autoimmune diseases. Furthermore, ANA levels do not consistently correlate well with disease activity hence they are more useful for diagnosis rather than monitoring of SLE.

Anti-Sm titres
Anti-Sm titres, referring to antibodies against Smith antigen, are specific for SLE but only found in about 30% of patients. Similar to ANA titres, Anti-Sm does not correlate well with disease severity or activity hence they are more used for diagnostic purposes rather than monitoring disease progression or flares.

stem: A 65-year-old woman attends the rheumatology clinic following a low-impact wrist fracture. A DEXA scan is performed, and her T score at the femoral neck is -2.6. She asks what this value means. Which statement best explains the basis of the T score measurement?
options: It compares her bone mass to that of young adults
It adjusts for age, gender, and ethnicity
It reflects risk of future fractures only
It measures bone turnover markers directly
It compares her bone mass to people of similar age
explanation:
It compares her bone mass to that of young adults
DEXA scans: the T score is based on bone mass of young reference population. It compares her bone mass to that of young adults: This is correct. The T score from a DEXA scan represents how many standard deviations a patient’s bone mineral density (BMD) is above or below the mean BMD of a healthy young adult reference population (typically aged 20–30). This approach allows clinicians to quantify osteoporosis risk based on how much a patient's bones have deviated from peak bone mass, which occurs in youth. In UK clinical practice, this underpins both diagnosis and management decisions: a T score ≤-2.5 defines osteoporosis according to WHO criteria.

It adjusts for age, gender, and ethnicity
This describes the Z score rather than the T score. The Z score assesses BMD relative to an age-matched population with similar demographic characteristics but does not form the basis for diagnosing osteoporosis in postmenopausal women or men over 50.

It reflects risk of future fractures only
While lower T scores are associated with increased fracture risk, the T score itself is specifically a statistical comparison to young adult mean BMD; it does not directly measure fracture risk alone but provides information used alongside other factors in risk assessment tools such as FRAX.

It measures bone turnover markers directly
Bone turnover markers are biochemical tests (e.g., serum CTX or P1NP), not imaging-based indices like the DEXA-derived T score. The T score is purely based on radiological assessment.

It compares her bone mass to people of similar age
This again refers to the Z score rather than the T score. For diagnostic purposes in older adults, clinicians rely on how far BMD has fallen compared with youthful peak values—not peers—because this better predicts fragility.

stem: An 80-year-old woman is started on oral alendronate following a fractured neck of femur. How would you explain how to take the tablet?
options: Take it on a full stomach to minimise gastric irritation and avoid lying down for 30 minutes afterwards
Dissolve tablet in water and take just before breakfast + sit up right for 30 minutes following
Take during main evening meal + sit up right for 2 hours following
Take at least 30 minutes before breakfast with plenty of water + sit up right for 30 minutes following
Take at least 30 minutes after a main meal + sit up right for 30 minutes following
explanation:
Take at least 30 minutes before breakfast with plenty of water + sit up right for 30 minutes following
Alendronate is a bisphosphonate used in the treatment of osteoporosis. It has poor oral bioavailability, which can be further reduced by food or drink (other than plain water). The absorption of alendronate is best when taken on an empty stomach, at least 30 minutes before the first food or drink of the day. Furthermore, due to its potential for causing oesophageal irritation and ulceration, it is recommended that patients remain upright (sitting or standing) for at least 30 minutes after ingestion to facilitate passage through the oesophagus.

Take it on a full stomach to minimise gastric irritation and avoid lying down for 30 minutes afterwards
This statement is incorrect because taking alendronate with food significantly decreases its absorption. While avoiding lying down for 30 minutes afterwards is correct, it should be taken on an empty stomach.

Dissolve tablet in water and take just before breakfast + sit up right for 30 minutes following
This statement is incorrect as alendronate tablets should not be dissolved in water before consumption. They must be swallowed whole with plenty of water to avoid oesophageal irritation.

Take during main evening meal + sit up right for 2 hours following
This statement is incorrect because taking alendronate during meals reduces its absorption. Although remaining upright for two hours would not cause harm, UK guidelines recommend remaining upright for only 30 minutes post-ingestion.

Take at least 30 minutes after a main meal + sit up right for 30 minutes following
This statement is incorrect as taking alendronate after meals will reduce its absorption. It should be taken at least half an hour before the first food or drink of the day.

stem: A 45-year-old refugee from Sudan presents for the first time since arriving in the UK to her GP with a swollen right lower leg. She states it became suddenly swollen yesterday morning. She has a copy of her medical record from Sudan which states she has had three previous lower limb DVTs, an episode of Budd-Chiari syndrome and four previous miscarriages. On examination, there is tenderness of the venous distribution of the right leg and a non-blanching reticulated rash throughout both lower limbs. A thorough examination is otherwise normal. What antibody is most specific for the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Anti-beta2 glycoprotein I
Antiphospholipid syndrome: arterial/venous thrombosis, miscarriage, livedo reticularis. This patient has recurrent venous thromboembolism (previous DVTs and an episode of hepatic vein thrombosis), recurrent foetal loss and a rash which is characteristic of livedo reticularis. These are common features of antiphospholipid syndrome. Anti-cardiolipin antibodies and anti-beta2 glycoprotein I antibodies are specific to this condition. You may also expect thrombocytopenia and a prolonged APTT.

Anti-U1 ribonucleoprotein antibodies
Anti-U1 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) antibodies are associated with mixed connective tissue disease which is a rare condition characterised by Raynaud's phenomenon, polyarthralgia, myalgia and other multisystem manifestations such as pericarditis. There is no association between mixed connective tissue disease and venous thromboembolism (VTE), livedo reticularis or recurrent miscarriage.

Anti-centromere antibodies
Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with limited systemic sclerosis of which CREST syndrome is a subtype. There is no evidence in this scenario of scleroderma of the face and distal limbs or the other features of CREST syndrome. Limited systemic sclerosis is not associated with VTE, livedo reticularis or recurrent miscarriage.

Anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA)
Anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) are a non-specific test which is not used in the diagnosis of antiphospholipid syndrome. It may be positive in rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, scleroderma and other conditions.

Antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA)
Antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) are associated with a heterogenous group of small vessel vasculitides including granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis. Microscopic polyangiitis can cause palpable purpura which is a non-blanching purpuric rash of the lower limbs, but this is distinct from livedo reticularis. All three conditions can lead to nephrotic syndrome which predisposes to VTE via loss of antithrombin III but there is no suggestion in the scenario of peripheral oedema. There is also no association between ANCA vasculitides and recurrent foetal loss or livedo reticularis.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents with a 12-month history of progressively worsening back pain. The pain and stiffness are worse in the morning and improve with exercise. You note the presence of a flexural rash with poorly defined areas of erythema, dry skin and lichenification. Observations are normal. Blood results are as follows: ESR 84 mm/hr (0-22) CRP 6 mg/L (0-10) ANA Negative RhF Negative Anti-CCP Negative What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ankylosing spondylitis
Ankylosing spondylitis is the correct answer. This is a classical presentation of a young male with lower back pain and stiffness of insidious onset, which is worse in the morning and moves with exercise. The markedly raised ESR further supports this.

Psoriatic arthritis
Psoriatic arthritis is incorrect. The rash present in the clinical case is a classic description of dermatitis rather than psoriasis. Characteristic psoriatic lesions are well-circumscribed erythematous plaques with silvery-white scales, typically distributed over extensor surfaces, especially favouring the elbows and knees, as well as the scalp.

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is incorrect. This is a common cause of back pain in older patients, however, in a patient of this age, it would be extremely unlikely. Furthermore, the clinical history and raised ESR are more supportive of an inflammatory condition.

Reactive arthritis
Reactive arthritis is incorrect. Reactive arthritis is characterised by the classic triad of arthritis, urethritis and, conjunctivitis. However, a majority of patients do not present with the classic triad. It is also a type of seronegative spondyloarthropathies. It usually self-resolves within 6 months. The duration of symptoms and absence of urethritis or conjunctivitis make this a less likely diagnosis.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. The negative RhF and anti-CCP make rheumatoid arthritis less likely, but not impossible since seronegative rheumatoid arthritis can occur. Regardless of this, the clinical and epidemiological features are more in keeping with ankylosing spondylitis.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a history of repeated episodes of muscle cramping, weakness, and dark-coloured urine following short bursts of intense physical activity such as sprinting or weightlifting. He notes that his symptoms typically resolve with rest. He has no fever, joint pain, or recent infections, and his physical examination is unremarkable. What is the most likely underlying mechanism for this man's condition?
options: Reduced calcium reuptake in sarcoplasmic reticulum
Sodium channel mutation causing hyperkalemic periodic paralysis
explanation:
Deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase
Repeated cramping, rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria after short bouts of exercise can point towards McArdle's disease. Deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase is the correct answer. This condition, known as McArdle's disease (glycogen storage disease type V), results from a deficiency in muscle glycogen phosphorylase, an enzyme essential for the degradation of glycogen to glucose during anaerobic, high-intensity exercise. In the absence of adequate glycogenolysis, muscles are unable to meet the energy demands of such activities, leading to symptoms such as cramping, fatigue, and myopathy. The release of myoglobin secondary to muscle breakdown accounts for the dark-coloured urine observed in this patient. The onset of symptoms in response to short-duration, high-intensity exercise is consistent with the pathophysiology associated with defects in glycogen breakdown.

Impaired fatty acid beta-oxidation
Impaired fatty acid beta-oxidation is incorrect because disorders affecting fatty acid oxidation, including carnitine palmitoyltransferase II (CPT II) deficiency, typically manifest with muscle symptoms following prolonged periods of low-intensity exercise or fasting rather than brief episodes of intense exertion. These conditions involve an inability to utilise fatty acids for energy during extended periods of metabolic demand. Given that this patient's presentation involves symptom onset after short bursts of intense activity, it does not correlate with impaired fatty acid beta-oxidation.

Mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation defect
Mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation defect is incorrect since mitochondrial dysfunctions compromise ATP production and often result in progressive weakness and generalised exercise intolerance rather than episodic symptoms. Moreover, mitochondrial disorders frequently affect multiple organ systems including ocular and neurological domains. However, the acute nature of this patient's symptoms occurring specifically post-intense exercise suggests a localised defect in energy metabolism rather than a widespread mitochondrial pathology.

Reduced calcium reuptake in sarcoplasmic reticulum
Reduced calcium reuptake in the sarcoplasmic reticulum is incorrect as diseases such as Brody myopathy arise from compromised calcium reuptake and lead predominantly to exercise-induced muscle stiffness due to difficulties with muscular relaxation. They do not characteristically cause muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) or dark urine as presented in this case. Additionally, Brody myopathy does not have a well-established link with short-duration high-intensity exercise as a principal precipitant.

Sodium channel mutation causing hyperkalemic periodic paralysis
Sodium channel mutation causing hyperkalemic periodic paralysis is incorrect because hyperkalemic periodic paralysis, which involves mutations in the SCN4A gene, presents primarily with episodes of muscle weakness triggered by specific factors like rest following physical activity, fasting or elevated potassium intake. Unlike McArdle’s disease, it does not typically result in muscle cramping or rhabdomyolysis nor does it produce dark-coloured urine. As this condition is not associated with defective glycogen metabolism pathways; it is unlikely to account for the clinical features seen in this patient.

stem: A 50-year-old man presented with gradual onset low backache for 2 years. There was no history of any chronic illness or alcoholism. His clinical examination revealed lumbar spine tenderness with a soft and non-tender abdomen. A bone scan revealed the presence of intense abnormal activity within the skull, lower thoracic and lumbar vertebrae as well as his pelvic bones. Biopsy performed of the L3 vertebra demonstrated trabeculae of cortical and cancellous bone with fibrotic marrow. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following would be elevated?
explanation:
Urinary hydroxyproline
Paget's disease - increased serum and urine levels of hydroxyproline. Urinary hydroxyproline is an adequate bone marker and in situations where there are very high rates of bone turnover, such as Paget's disease of bone which is the diagnosis here, its level is increased.

Urinary coproporphyrin
Urinary coproporphyrin is incorrect as its excretion is increased in patients with Dubin-Johnson syndrome to a greater degree than in patients with other hepatobiliary disorders. Given the absence of jaundice in this patient, this diagnosis is unlikely.

Urinary delta-aminolevulinic acid
Urinary delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) excretion will also be raised in urine samples from individuals with acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), but the measurement is less widely available and is not essential. AIP is a rare metabolic disorder that is characterised by severe abdominal pain, muscle weakness, irritability, vomiting and constipation - not seen in this case.

Urinary porphobilinogen
Urinary porphobilinogen is incorrect as this is increased in acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), a rare metabolic disorder that is characterised by severe abdominal pain, muscle weakness, irritability, vomiting and constipation - not seen in this case.

Urinary uroporphyrin
Urinary uroporphyrin levels are high in porphyria cutanea tarda, which occurs due to uroporphyrin decarboxylase deficiency. Porphyria cutanea tarda is a rare disorder characterised by painful, blistering skin lesions that develop on sun-exposed skin, which is not described in this case.

stem: A 34-year-old female with a history of discoid lupus erythematous is reviewed in clinic. The erythematous, scaly rash on her face has not responded to topical steroid creams. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Oral hydroxychloroquine
Hydroxychloroquine is an antimalarial drug that has immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory effects. It is the first-line treatment for cutaneous lupus erythematosus, including discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE), according to the British Association of Dermatologists guidelines. It helps in reducing inflammation and skin lesions associated with DLE. Its use should be monitored by an ophthalmologist due to the risk of retinopathy.

UV light therapy
UV light therapy is not a suitable option for this patient. UV exposure can exacerbate symptoms in patients with DLE as they often have photosensitivity, which means their condition worsens on exposure to sunlight or artificial sources of UV light.

Topical dapsone
Topical dapsone may be considered for some forms of cutaneous lupus, but it is not typically first-line therapy and would not be the next step after failure of topical steroids in DLE management.

Oral prednisolone
Oral prednisolone could potentially be used in severe cases where there are systemic symptoms or if other treatments fail. However, it's not generally recommended as a long-term treatment due to its side effect profile. It would also typically not be the next step after failure of topical steroids.

Topical hydroxychloroquine
Topical hydroxychloroquine is not commonly used or recommended in the management of DLE. Oral administration allows for systemic absorption and action, which is generally more effective for controlling symptoms across all affected areas rather than just locally treating areas where a cream has been applied.

stem: A 28-year-old man is diagnosed with having ankylosing spondylitis. He presented with a six month history of back pain. On examination there is reduced lateral flexion of the spine but no evidence of any other complications. Which one of the following is he most likely to offered as first-line treatment?
explanation:
Exercise regime + NSAIDs
Exercise regimes and NSAIDs are the 1st line management for ankylosing spondylitis

Exercise regime + infliximab
The anti-TNF drugs are currently only used for patients with severe ankylosing spondylitis which has failed to respond to NSAIDs.

stem: You are asked to see a 32-year-old man by the trauma and orthopaedic team, who presented with a broken femur following a seemingly innocuous trip at home. Looking through his records, they have noted several fractures in the past, and have organised blood tests which are shown below. He tells you his mother also has a history of multiple fractures from minor falls. Calcium 2.4 mmol/L (2.1-2.6) Phosphate 1.1 mmol/L (0.8-1.4) ALP 50 u/L (30 - 100) PTH 55 pg/mL (14-65) An x-ray of his pelvis was reported to have a 'bone within a bone' appearance. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Osteopetrosis
This is describing a case of osteopetrosis, which is a rare condition characterised by increased bone density within abnormal bone architecture, which causes paradoxical brittleness of the bones. There are various types with various inheritance patterns, with autosomal dominant being the most common. Calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and parathyroid hormones (PTH) levels are normal in this condition.

Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis is another cause of fragility fractures but is very uncommon in otherwise healthy 32-year-old men. The main risk factors include increasing age, female sex, smoking, poor nutritional intake, chronic steroid use, and renal failure.

Primary hyperparathyroidism
Primary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. Usually caused by an adenoma, these tumours secrete PTH, resulting in elevated PTH and calcium levels. Symptoms are typically those linked to hypercalcaemia. In this case, neither the biochemical markers nor the symptomatology suggests primary hyperparathyroidism as the cause of this man's presentation.

Paget's disease of the bone
Paget's disease of the bone is the main distractor in this question. It is also a condition characterised by abnormal bone remodelling, can cause fragility fractures, and is often asymptomatic, but typically features raised ALP levels. These are not seen in this case. It is also uncommon in those below 55.

Hypervitaminosis D
Hypervitaminosis D is almost always caused by excessive and prolonged vitamin D supplementation and causes hypercalcaemia and its associated symptoms. It is therefore incorrect in this question.

stem: A 36-year-old woman presents with progressive tingling and numbness of the 4th and 5th fingers of her right hand. Initially, this was intermittent but recently has become constant. She notices that the symptoms are worse when leaning on her right elbow. She recalls hitting her elbow against a door some time ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cubital tunnel syndrome
Cubital tunnel syndrome is caused by compression of the ulnar nerve and can present with tingling/numbness of the 4th and 5th finger. The ulnar nerve runs through the cubital tunnel and compression of this will lead to the symptoms described - tingling and numbness of the 4th and 5th fingers. Management is often conservative but surgery may be required.

Carpal tunnel syndrome
Carpal tunnel syndrome is due to compression of the median nerve at the wrist, where it runs through the carpal tunnel. This would present with generalised pain and tingling of the hand and wrist, not specifically the 4th and 5th fingers.

De Quervain's tenosynovitis
De Quervain's tenosynovitis would present differently, with pain on movement of the thumb/wrist. The radial styloid may be hardened and thickened.

Medial epicondylitis
Medial epicondylitis, or golfer's elbow, would present with pain along the medial elbow, close to the cubital tunnel - but localised to the area as it is a tendinopathy, and not compression of the nerve.

Radial tunnel syndrome
Radial tunnel syndrome, as the name suggests, is due to compression of the radial nerve and may lead to tingling/numbness/pain along the back of the hand and forearm.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a six-month history of joint pain and swelling, predominantly affecting the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of his fingers of both hands. He reports worsening discomfort first thing in the mornings with some mild improvement with activity. On examination, there is visible swelling and tenderness in the DIP joints, along with sausage-like swelling of the fingers. He denies any recent trauma or infections and has no known significant past medical history. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Psoriatic arthritis
