The average bone mass of a population of the same age and sex is not used as the reference standard for T-scores in DEXA scans; rather, it pertains to Z-scores. The Z-score compares an individual's bone density with that of others who are similar in age, sex, and body size. Although useful for evaluating bone density in younger individuals or when exploring secondary causes of bone loss, the Z-score is not suitable in this context.

Average bone mass of a population with similar medical conditions
The average bone mass of a population with similar medical conditions does not form the basis for calculating the T-score in DEXA scans. Instead, the T-score juxtaposes an individual's bone mass with that of healthy young adults irrespective of any health conditions they may have. Utilising comparisons with populations sharing similar medical conditions would not accurately reflect changes in bone density due to normal ageing or osteoporotic processes.

Bone mass of elderly individuals
The bone mass of elderly individuals is not utilised when interpreting T-scores from DEXA scans because these scores are intended to compare an individual’s bone density with that of healthy young adults rather than older people. Such methodology is essential for detecting significant reductions in bone mass indicative of osteoporosis since age-related bone loss is anticipated and would seem less pronounced if contrasted with an elderly reference group. Therefore, employing older individuals as a benchmark could obscure decreases in bone density and complicate osteoporosis diagnosis.

Bone mass of patients with a known history of osteoporosis
Referencing the bone mass of patients with a known history of osteoporosis is unsuitable for determining T-scores since these scores rely on comparisons with healthy young adults' baseline values. The objective behind using T-scores is to discern deviations from normalcy in bone density to detect either osteoporosis or osteopenia. Using individuals already diagnosed with osteoporosis as a comparative measure would conceal true levels of bone loss relative to a healthy norm and impair the accurate assessment of condition severity.

stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with pain in her right hand and forearm which has been getting worse for the past few weeks. There is no history of trauma. The pain is concentrated around the thumb and index finger and is often worse at night. Shaking her hand seems to provide some relief. On examination there is weakness of the abductor pollicis brevis and reduced sensation to fine touch at the index finger. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Carpal tunnel syndrome
Patients with carpal tunnel syndrome often get relief from shaking their hands and this may be an important clue in exam questions.

C6 entrapment neuropathy
More proximal symptoms would be expected with a C6 entrapment neuropathy e.g. weakness of the biceps muscle or reduced biceps reflex.

stem: You review a 40-year-old mechanic who presents with joint pains. For the past two months he has noticed intermittent pain, stiffness and swelling of the joints in his hands and feet. The stiffness tends to improve during the day but the pain tends to get worse. He has also noticed stiffness in his back but cannot remember any aggravating injury. You order some blood tests (taken during an acute attack) which are reported as follows: Rheumatoid factor Negative Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody Positive Uric acid 0.3 mmol/l (0.18 - 0.48) ESR 41 mm/hr What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Rheumatoid arthritis
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies are associated with rheumatoid arthritis. The correct answer is Rheumatoid arthritis. This is a chronic, systemic inflammatory disorder that primarily affects joints. It may result in swollen, painful joints and can lead to joint destruction and functional disability. The patient's symptoms of intermittent pain, stiffness, and swelling in the hands and feet are characteristic of rheumatoid arthritis. Additionally, the presence of anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies is highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis. While rheumatoid factor is often positive in this condition, it can also be negative especially early in the disease course.

Reactive arthritis
Reactive arthritis is typically a consequence of an infection elsewhere in the body such as the genitourinary or gastrointestinal tract. Its onset is usually acute with asymmetric lower limb oligoarthritis being common. There are no specific blood tests for reactive arthritis but it does not typically present with anti-CCP antibodies.

Ankylosing spondylitis
Ankylosing spondylitis primarily affects the axial skeleton causing inflammatory back pain which improves with exercise but not rest. Peripheral joint involvement can occur but it tends to affect lower limbs more than upper limbs. While patients may have raised ESR during active disease, they would not usually have anti-CCP antibodies.

Gout
Gout typically presents as an acute monoarthritis affecting the first metatarsophalangeal joint (big toe). The patient's uric acid level was within normal range which makes gout less likely. Furthermore, gout would not cause anti-CCP antibody positivity.

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis, a degenerative joint disease due to wear and tear of cartilage, commonly affects weight-bearing joints like knees and hips or hands (DIPs & PIPs), but it doesn't cause systemic symptoms or morning stiffness lasting for several hours, unlike rheumatoid arthritis. Blood tests including ESR and anti-CCP antibody would be normal in osteoarthritis.

stem: A 48-year-old patient presented to her family physician complaining of pain all over her body for the past 4 months. She initially thought it was because she started taking aerobic exercise classes 6 months ago. However, the pain has been persistently bothering her and taking over-the-counter pain relievers did not help. The pain is more pronounced around her shoulders and lower back. She also complains feeling tired and not being able to sleep because of the pain. She has a body mass index of 28 kg per m2 and has never smoked in her life. She denies any weight loss or episodes of fever. She currently lives alone and is usually able to do her household chores. Her mother who passed away last year suffered from rheumatoid arthritis. On examination, the doctor finds that the patient has tender areas on her neck, elbow regions, and knees. Which is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
explanation:
Fibromyalgia
This patient presented with a chronic pain described as all over her body for the past 6 months. The pain did not appear to be originating from the joints and therefore this makes a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis unlikely. The two most likely diagnoses are fibromyalgia and polymyalgia rheumatica. However, polymyalgia rheumatica would have also presented with weight loss and fever. This patient most likely has fibromyalgia. She also feels tired and suffers from sleep disturbances, which are both common complaints in patients suffering from fibromyalgia.

Polymyalgia rheumatica
Polymyalgia rheumatica would have also presented with weight loss and fever. This patient does not have these symptoms.

Polymyositis
There is no history of muscle weakness in this patient. Muscle weakness in the shoulder region would have made a diagnosis of polymyositis likely.

Ankylosing spondylitis
This is an inflammatory musculoskeletal condition which most affects the axial skeleton. It is strongly associated with HLA-B27 histocompatibility complex. The first presentation is usually a pain in the lower back region due to sacroiliitis. This patient does not have specific axial skeleton involvement.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is a common painful inflammatory musculoskeletal condition affecting the joints. It is an autoimmune condition which usually affects the small joints of the hands and feet in a symmetric distribution. Patients often develop deformities such as ulnar deviation as the disease progresses and articular structures are destroyed. The pain in this patient does not appear to be originating from the joints.

stem: A 43-year-old woman presents with pain in the right elbow. This has been present for the past month and she reports no obvious trigger. On examination she reports pain on wrist extension against resistance whilst the elbow is extended. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lateral epicondylitis
The most likely diagnosis in this case is lateral epicondylitis, also known as tennis elbow. This condition is characterized by pain and tenderness over the lateral epicondyle of the humerus, which is aggravated by wrist extension against resistance with the elbow extended. The patient's presentation of pain in the right elbow without an obvious trigger and positive findings on examination are consistent with lateral epicondylitis.

Cubital tunnel syndrome
Cubital tunnel syndrome is caused by compression of the ulnar nerve at the level of the elbow, leading to symptoms such as numbness and tingling in the ring and little fingers, as well as weakness in hand grip. However, this patient does not report any sensory or motor symptoms, making cubital tunnel syndrome less likely.

Carpal tunnel syndrome
Carpal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the median nerve at the level of the wrist. Symptoms typically include numbness, tingling, and pain in the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and half of the ring finger. Patients may also experience nocturnal symptoms that are relieved by shaking their hands. The absence of these specific symptoms makes carpal tunnel syndrome an unlikely diagnosis for this patient.

Medial epicondylitis
Medial epicondylitis, or golfer's elbow, involves pain and tenderness over the medial epicondyle of the humerus. Pain is usually elicited by resisted wrist flexion with pronation while keeping the elbow flexed 90 degrees or resisted forearm pronation with the elbow extended. Since this patient reports pain on wrist extension rather than flexion or pronation, medial epicondylitis is not a likely diagnosis.

Pronator syndrome
Pronator syndrome occurs due to entrapment of the median nerve between two heads of the pronator teres muscle or under the fibrous arch formed by flexor digitorum superficialis muscle leading to pain in the proximal forearm and sometimes paresthesia in the median nerve distribution. However, this patient's symptoms are more localized to the elbow and are aggravated by wrist extension, making pronator syndrome less likely.

stem: A 39-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 3-month history of worsening lower back pain. He denies any trauma or prior fractures. He takes no medications, does not smoke, consume excessive alcohol, and had never been treated with corticosteroids. A review of systems demonstrates delayed puberty with reduced libido for several years and absence of morning erections. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scans of the skeleton is reported below using Z-scores. Lumbar vertebrae (L2-L4) -6.9 Femoral neck -3.5 Total hip -4 What test would be crucial to perform alongside routine investigations?
explanation:
Testosterone
Osteoporosis in a man - check testosterone. Testosterone blood tests are important when suspecting osteoporosis in a man. Hypogonadism is a common cause of osteoporosis in men. It is classified either as hypergonadotropic (primary gonadal failure) or hypogonadotropic (secondary to a defect in the hypothalamic-pituitary axis) hypogonadism. The role of androgens on male bone metabolism is twofold. First, androgens stimulate bone formation during puberty. Second, androgens prevent bone resorption during and after puberty.

Alpha fetoprotein
Alpha fetoprotein (AFP) is a marker that may be elevated in association with a variety of malignancies or benign diseases. Maternal AFP serum level is used to screen for Down syndrome, neural tube defects. It is not valuable in evaluating osteoporosis.

Serum calcitonin
Calcitonin is a tumor marker. Tumor markers are substances made by cancer cells or by normal cells in response to cancer in the body. If too much calcitonin is found in the blood, it may be a sign of a type of thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid cancer.

Serum protein electrophoresis
Serum protein electrophoresis is used to identify patients with multiple myeloma and other serum protein disorders. Electrophoresis separates proteins based on their physical properties, and the subsets of these proteins are used in interpreting the results. Given the lumbar back pain, this test would be useful to perform and exclude multiple myeloma but is unlikely given his age.

Urinary hydroxyproline
Urinary hydroxyproline is an adequate bone marker and in situations where there are very high rates of bone turnover, such as Paget's disease of the bone its level is increased. This is not suggestive here based on the history and DEXA findings making this answer incorrect.

stem: A 50-year-old diabetic right-handed lady presents with left shoulder pain. She describes a stiff shoulder often more painful at night and has difficulty dressing or doing up her bra. On examination, there is no point tenderness and you notice weakness in external rotation. What is the most likely cause of her shoulder pain?
explanation:
Adhesive capsulitis
External rotation (on both active and passive movement) is classically impaired in adhesive capsulitis. Adhesive capsulitis presents as a painful stiff shoulder with restriction of active and passive range of motion in abduction, internal and external rotation. However, external rotation often shows the most marked restriction and is the first movement to show impairment. The stem describes difficulty dressing and doing up her bra as well as weakness of external rotation suggesting a globally impaired range of motion. Patients often report difficulty sleeping on the affected side. Other indications that the answer is adhesive capsulitis include coexisting diabetes, female gender, and symptoms in the non-dominant hand, all of which are common findings in this condition.

Acromioclavicular degeneration
Acromioclavicular degeneration is often associated with popping, swelling, clicking, or grindings and a positive scarf test not reported in the stem.

Subacromial impingement
Subacromial impingement patients often complain of pain on overhead activities and demonstrate a painful arc of abduction on examination worse between 90 and 120 degrees. There may also be popping, snapping, or grinding.

Rotator cuff tear
Rotator cuff tears can occur either due to specific trauma or chronic impingement. Patients will normally describe weakness as well as pain and there may be muscle wasting and tenderness on palpation. There may be a painful arc of movement and weakness of the affected muscle.

Calcific tendinopathy
Patients with calcific tendinopathy would normally have tenderness on palpation of the affected area and be reluctant to move the arm. There may be overlap with symptoms of impingement syndrome making this a less likely answer.

stem: A 70-year-old woman is reviewed. She sustained a fracture of her wrist one year ago, following which a DEXA scan was performed. This showed a T-score of -2.8 SD. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation was started along with oral alendronate. This however was stopped due to oesophagitis. In accordance with NICE guidelines, what is the most suitable next management step?
explanation:
Switch to risedronate
The correct answer is to switch to risedronate. According to NICE guidelines, in postmenopausal women who cannot tolerate oral alendronate, risedronate is the recommended second-line bisphosphonate. The patient's T-score of -2.8 SD indicates osteoporosis, and she has already sustained a fragility fracture, making her at high risk for future fractures. Risedronate, like alendronate, is a bisphosphonate that reduces fracture risk by inhibiting osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, but may be better tolerated due to slightly different molecular properties.

Start hormone replacement therapy
Starting hormone replacement therapy would be inappropriate in this 70-year-old woman. While HRT can help prevent bone loss, it is not recommended as first-line treatment for osteoporosis in women over 60 due to increased risks of breast cancer, venous thromboembolism, and cardiovascular events.

Start raloxifene
Starting raloxifene is not the most appropriate next step. While raloxifene (a selective oestrogen receptor modulator) can be used in postmenopausal osteoporosis, NICE guidelines recommend trying an alternative bisphosphonate first before considering other drug classes.

Start teriparatide
Starting teriparatide would not be appropriate at this stage. Teriparatide, a parathyroid hormone analogue, is reserved for patients with severe osteoporosis who have failed or are intolerant to multiple other treatments, due to its high cost and need for daily subcutaneous injections.

Refer for hip protectors
Referring for hip protectors alone would be insufficient management. While hip protectors may have a role in preventing hip fractures in high-risk individuals, they should not be used as an alternative to appropriate pharmacological therapy in someone with established osteoporosis.

stem: A 71-year-old man presents with an erythematous, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint on the left foot. This is causing him considerable pain and he is having difficulty walking. He has never had any previous similar episodes. His past medical history includes atrial fibrillation and type 2 diabetes mellitus and his current medications are warfarin, metformin and simvastatin. What is the most appropriate treatment of this episode?
explanation:
Colchicine
Colchicine is the most appropriate treatment for this episode.

Intra-articular corticosteroid
While anticoagulation is not a contraindication to joint injection, it would make this option less attractive.

Ibuprofen
NSAIDs should be avoided in elderly patients taking warfarin due to the risk of a life-threatening gastrointestinal haemorrhage.

Diclofenac
NSAIDs should be avoided in elderly patients taking warfarin due to the risk of a life-threatening gastrointestinal haemorrhage.

Prednisolone
Oral steroids are an option but would upset his diabetic control.

stem: A 40-year-old gardener presents with a 2-week history of gradually worsening pain in the left elbow. When the elbow is straight, the pain is worse on resisted wrist extension and supination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lateral epicondylitis
Lateral epicondylitis: worse on resisted wrist extension/suppination whilst elbow extended. The correct answer is lateral epicondylitis. This is caused by repetitive arm movements. Typically, the pain is worse on wrist extension against resistance, when the elbow is straightened.

Anterior interosseous syndrome
Anterior interosseous syndrome is caused by damage to the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. It usually presents with pain in the forearm and weakness of flexion of the index finger and the distal phalanx of the thumb.

Carpal tunnel syndrome
The description is not typical of carpal tunnel syndrome, which would characteristically present with numbness or altered sensation, and/or pain in the distribution of the median nerve.

Medial epicondylitis
Medial epicondylitis is also known as golfer's elbow. Pain is worse on flexion and pronation of the wrist.

Olecranon bursitis
Olecranon bursitis characteristically presents with both pain and swelling over the tip of the elbow.

stem: A 50-year-old female with a history of rheumatoid presents with a suspected septic knee joint. A diagnostic aspiration is performed and sent to microbiology. Which of the following organisms is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus
The correct answer is Staphylococcus aureus. This organism is the most common cause of septic arthritis in adults. It can enter the bloodstream from a distant site and then infect the joint, or it can be introduced directly into the joint during trauma or surgery. In patients with rheumatoid arthritis, damage to the joint lining can also increase susceptibility to infection.

Staphylococcus epidermidis
Staphylococcus epidermidis is less likely to be responsible for septic arthritis in this patient. While it is a common skin commensal and can cause infection following prosthetic joint surgery, it's not typically associated with septic arthritis in native joints.

Escherichia coli
Escherichia coli, while a common cause of urinary tract infections and abdominal sepsis, is not often found as a causative agent in septic arthritis. However, in patients with risk factors such as diabetes mellitus or immunosuppression, Gram-negative organisms like E.coli may indeed be implicated.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Neisseria gonorrhoeae could potentially cause a septic knee joint but this is more likely in sexually active younger individuals rather than a 50-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis. Gonococcal arthritis often presents differently too, typically as part of a syndrome that includes tenosynovitis, dermatitis and migratory polyarthralgia.

Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniae is an unlikely culprit for this patient's condition. While S.pneumoniae does occasionally cause joint infections, these are rare and usually occur after bacteremia from pneumococcal pneumonia or meningitis. It's much less commonly seen as a cause of septic arthritis compared to Staphylococcus aureus.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is referred to the rheumatology outpatient clinic with polyarthralgia affecting her hands and feet. She has no past medical history and does not take any regular medications. She does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. She lives with her family and works as a hairdresser. On examination, there is no evidence of synovitis but her fingers and toes are noted to be dusky and blue, without evidence of ulceration. There is proximal pain and tenderness with power 4+/5 at the shoulders and hips bilaterally. There is no evidence of oral or nasal ulceration, skin hardening or rashes. Chest auscultation reveals bibasal end-inspiratory crackles, which do not clear on coughing. The jugular venous pulse is not raised, the pulmonary component of the second heart sound is normal and there is no peripheral oedema. Urinalysis is unremarkable. Plain radiography of the chest demonstrates reticular changes at the bases. Blood tests: Hb 137 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 189 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 4.5 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Na+ 136 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 5.4 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 89 µmol/L (55 - 120) CRP 4 mg/L (< 5) C3 1.46 g/L (0.9-1.8) C4 0.21 g/L (0.1-0.4) Double-stranded DNA antibodies 1.2 IU/ml (1-10) Creatine kinase 444 IU/L (25-200) Further blood tests: Anti-CCP antibodies negative Rheumatoid factor negative Anti-Ro negative Anti-La negative Anti-Jo1 negative Anti-ribonuclear protein antibody positive Anti-Smith antibody negative HIV negative Hepatitis B sAg negative Hepatitis C Ab negative Anti-Scl-70 antibody negative Anti-centromere antibody negative What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Mixed connective tissue disease
Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) is the correct answer. This is a connective tissue disease that has classically been described as having features of multiple connective tissue diseases (CTD) (e.g. myositis, scleroderma, Sjogren's, SLE) and an association with anti-ribonuclear protein (anti-RNP) antibody. This patient has Raynaud's, myositis, polyarthralgia and clinical evidence of interstitial lung disease in addition to the characteristic antibody.

Dermatomyositis
Dermatomyositis is incorrect. This patient does not have the classic skin features of dermatomyositis e.g. shawl sign, Gottron's papules, heliotrope rash.

Scleroderma
Scleroderma is incorrect. The typical skin features of scleroderma are absent. While it is possible to have scleroderma without typical skin hardening, the presentation in this case with features of multiple CTDs with anti-RNP antibodies favours MCTD.

Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis
Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. This patient has polyarthralgia rather than synovitis and myositis and Raynaud's are not typical features of rheumatoid arthritis.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus is incorrect. A positive ANA, myositis, polyarthralgia and Raynaud's can be features of SLE. However, the absence of more specific lupus features e.g. anti-Smith antibody, hypocomplementemia and double-stranded DNA raise suspicion of another diagnosis in this context. Furthermore, interstitial lung disease is less common in SLE.

stem: A 24-year-old man reports a 1-year history of increasing low back pain. He reports that the symptoms are usually worse after being sedentary. There is also stiffness in this area that can last up to 30 minutes in the morning. He is normally a keen footballer and gym-goer and finds that both of these actually improve his pain levels. However, he has been increasingly troubled by pain in his right Achilles tendon which has limited his activity levels. His GP has referred him to a rheumatologist and has arranged lumbar spine and sacroiliac joint x-rays in the meantime. Which of these collection of findings are most likely to be seen?
options: Block vertebra and excessive lumbar lordosis
Joint space narrowing, osteophytes and subchondral cysts
Marginal erosions, soft tissue swelling and periarticular osteoporosis
Soft tissue swelling, punched-out bone lesions and overhanging sclerotic margins
Subchondral erosions, sclerosis and squaring of vertebrae
explanation:
Subchondral erosions, sclerosis and squaring of vertebrae
Ankylosing spondylitis - x-ray findings: subchondral erosions, sclerosis and squaring of lumbar vertebrae. This man has typical features of ankylosing spondylitis: low back pain which is worse at rest and improves on activity, early morning stiffness exceeding 15 minutes in duration, and associated Achilles tendinopathy (enthesitis). Onset is most common in males between 20-30 years of age. Plain radiography commonly shows subchondral erosions and sclerosis affecting the sacroiliac joints (sacroiliitis). In the lumbar spine, abnormalities such as vertebral body squaring, ligament calcification and syndesmophytes may be seen, eventually leading to the formation of a 'bamboo spine'.

Block vertebra and excessive lumbar lordosis
Block vertebra describes an anatomic variant where there is a failure of separation of two or more adjacent vertebral bodies. Excessive lumbar lordosis is not seen in ankylosing spondylitis - in fact, the opposite is true.

Joint space narrowing, osteophytes and subchondral cysts
Joint space narrowing, osteophytes and subchondral cysts are hallmark radiographic appearances of osteoarthritis.

Marginal erosions, soft tissue swelling and periarticular osteoporosis
Marginal erosions, soft tissue swelling and periarticular osteoporosis are seen in rheumatoid arthritis.

Soft tissue swelling, punched-out bone lesions and overhanging sclerotic margins
Soft tissue swelling, punched-out bone lesions and overhanging sclerotic margins are seen in gout.

stem: A 62-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis, managed with weekly methotrexate, presents to the emergency department with fever, sore throat, and mouth ulcers. He was recently prescribed an antibiotic for a urinary tract infection. His blood tests show pancytopenia. Hb 89 g/L (135-180) Platelets 45 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 1.1 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Neutrophils 0.4 * 109/L (2.0 - 7.5) The prescribed antibiotic has potentiated methotrexate toxicity by acting on the same enzymatic pathway. Which enzyme is inhibited by both of these medications?
explanation:
Dihydrofolate reductase
Methotrexate works by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase. The clinical presentation of fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers (mucositis), and pancytopenia in a patient on methotrexate is highly suggestive of severe myelosuppression due to methotrexate toxicity. The question states this has been potentiated by a recently prescribed antibiotic. The antibiotic most implicated in this interaction is trimethoprim (often given as cotrimoxazole). Both methotrexate and trimethoprim are potent inhibitors of the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR). Methotrexate is a folate analogue and competitively inhibits DHFR, preventing the conversion of dihydrofolate to its active form, tetrahydrofolate. Tetrahydrofolate is essential for the synthesis of purines and pyrimidines, the building blocks of DNA and RNA. By inhibiting this pathway, methotrexate suppresses the proliferation of rapidly dividing cells, including lymphocytes (therapeutic effect) and bone marrow precursors (adverse effect). Trimethoprim also inhibits DHFR, and when co-prescribed, this leads to a synergistic and profound blockade of folate metabolism, resulting in life-threatening bone marrow aplasia. This combination is therefore contraindicated.

Cyclo-oxygenase
Cyclo-oxygenase (COX) is the enzyme inhibited by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and aspirin. While high-dose aspirin can increase methotrexate toxicity by reducing its renal excretion, the primary mechanism of action is not a shared inhibition of COX. NSAIDs are commonly used for symptomatic relief in rheumatoid arthritis, but their mechanism is distinct from that of methotrexate.

DNA gyrase
DNA gyrase is a topoisomerase enzyme that is the primary target of quinolone antibiotics, such as ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin. These antibiotics are used to treat urinary tract infections. While there is some evidence that quinolones can increase methotrexate levels by competing for renal tubular secretion, their fundamental mechanism of action is entirely different and does not involve the folate pathway. Therefore, they do not share the same target enzyme as methotrexate.

Thiopurine methyltransferase
Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) is an enzyme crucial for the metabolism of thiopurine drugs, such as azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine, which are also used in rheumatology and gastroenterology. Genetic deficiency in TPMT activity leads to a significantly increased risk of myelosuppression from these drugs. However, TPMT is not involved in the metabolism or mechanism of action of methotrexate or trimethoprim.

Xanthine oxidase
Xanthine oxidase is the enzyme responsible for the breakdown of purines to uric acid. It is inhibited by drugs like allopurinol, which is used to treat gout. A classic and important drug interaction occurs between allopurinol and azathioprine, as allopurinol inhibits the breakdown of azathioprine, leading to its toxic accumulation. This is a key interaction to be aware of in clinical practice, but it is not relevant to the mechanism of methotrexate toxicity.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the dermatology clinic with a 6-month history of well-demarcated, erythematous, scaly plaques on her cheeks and scalp. The lesions are worse after sun exposure. She has been using topical betamethasone 0.1% for 3 months with minimal improvement. Some areas on her scalp now show hair loss with scarring. She has no systemic symptoms. ANA is negative. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Oral hydroxychloroquine
Oral hydroxychloroquine is the most appropriate next step in management for this patient with discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) who has failed to respond adequately to topical steroids. The clinical presentation is classic for DLE with well-demarcated, erythematous, scaly plaques on sun-exposed areas (face and scalp), photosensitivity, and scarring alopecia. Antimalarials, particularly hydroxychloroquine, are considered the first-line systemic therapy for DLE when topical treatments are insufficient. Hydroxychloroquine typically works within 48 weeks and has a good safety profile with appropriate monitoring. The negative ANA is consistent with DLE, which often presents without systemic involvement or serological markers of systemic lupus erythematosus. Hydroxychloroquine not only treats the current lesions but may prevent new lesions and reduce photosensitivity.

Oral prednisolone
Oral prednisolone is not appropriate as first-line systemic therapy for DLE. Systemic corticosteroids are generally reserved for severe, rapidly progressive disease or when there are significant systemic features suggesting SLE. This patient has localized cutaneous disease without systemic symptoms. Long-term systemic steroids carry significant side effects including weight gain, diabetes, osteoporosis, and hypertension, making them unsuitable for chronic management of DLE.

Topical tacrolimus
Topical tacrolimus could be considered as an alternative topical therapy, particularly for facial lesions where prolonged use of potent topical steroids may cause skin atrophy. However, this patient has already failed topical therapy for 3 months and has developed scarring alopecia, indicating that progression to systemic therapy is warranted rather than trying another topical agent.

Oral methotrexate
Oral methotrexate is typically considered a third-line agent for DLE after failure of antimalarials and is usually reserved for refractory cases. It has a more significant side effect profile including hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, and teratogenicity, making it less suitable as a second-line agent in a young woman.

Phototherapy
Phototherapy is contraindicated in DLE as UV exposure can exacerbate the condition. The patient's history specifically mentions worsening after sun exposure, highlighting the photosensitive nature of her disease. Phototherapy could potentially trigger flares and lead to progression of the disease.

stem: A 28-year-old woman who has rheumatoid arthritis is to be started on etanercept injections after failing to respond to methotrexate and sulfsalazine. Which one of the following adverse effects is associated with the use of etanercept?
explanation:
Reactivation of tuberculosis
TNF-α inhibitors may reactivate TB. The correct answer is Reactivation of tuberculosis. Etanercept, a tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor, can lead to reactivation of latent tuberculosis (TB). This is because TNF plays a crucial role in granuloma formation and containment of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Therefore, inhibiting TNF can disrupt these granulomas and allow for reactivation of the disease. In the UK, guidelines recommend screening for latent TB before starting treatment with etanercept or other TNF inhibitors.

Triggering Churg-Strauss syndrome
Triggering Churg-Strauss syndrome is not associated with etanercept use. Churg-Strauss syndrome, also known as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), is an autoimmune condition that causes inflammation and damage to blood vessels. It's typically associated with asthma and high levels of eosinophils - a type of white blood cell. There's no evidence to suggest that etanercept triggers this syndrome.

Thrombocytosis
Thrombocytosis, an abnormally high platelet count, is not a recognised side effect of etanercept. Thrombocytosis can occur due to various conditions such as infection, inflammation, cancer or certain blood disorders but it's not linked directly to etanercept use.

Tendonitis
Regarding Tendonitis, while rheumatoid arthritis itself can cause tendinitis due to chronic inflammation, there's no clear evidence suggesting that etanercept increases the risk of developing tendonitis.

Cardiomyopathy
Cardiomyopathy, a disease of the heart muscle that makes it harder for your heart to pump blood to the rest of your body, is also not directly related to etanercept use. While rheumatoid arthritis patients have an increased risk for cardiovascular diseases due to systemic inflammation and other factors, this isn't specifically linked to the use of etanercept.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with a history of primary Sjogren's syndrome is reviewed in clinic. Her main problem is a dry mouth, which unfortunately has not responded to artificial saliva. Which one of the following medications is most likely to be beneficial?
explanation:
Pilocarpine
The correct answer in this case is Pilocarpine. Pilocarpine is a parasympathomimetic agent, which means it stimulates the parasympathetic nervous system. The parasympathetic nervous system is responsible for stimulating salivary gland secretion, among other functions. In patients with primary Sjogren's syndrome, the exocrine glands like the salivary glands are affected, leading to symptoms such as dry mouth (xerostomia). Pilocarpine can help alleviate xerostomia by increasing saliva production via its action on muscarinic receptors in the salivary glands.

Rivastigmine
Rivastigmine is a cholinesterase inhibitor used primarily in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease dementia. While it does increase acetylcholine levels in the brain, it has no significant effect on salivary gland function and would not be beneficial for treating dry mouth in Sjogren's syndrome.

Neostigmine
Neostigmine is another cholinesterase inhibitor that acts peripherally and has been used to treat myasthenia gravis and reverse neuromuscular blockade after surgery. However, its effects on salivation are less specific than pilocarpine and may cause unwanted side effects due to its broad action on various cholinergic synapses.

Clonidine
Clonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that acts centrally to lower blood pressure. It has been used for hypertension, opioid withdrawal symptoms, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Clonidine does not have any significant effect on saliva production or the management of xerostomia.

Atropine
Atropine is an antimuscarinic agent that blocks muscarinic receptors, which are responsible for the stimulation of salivary gland secretion. In fact, atropine would worsen dry mouth symptoms, as it is commonly used to reduce secretions in certain clinical situations such as preoperative care and palliative care.

stem: A 64-year-old man presents with acute-onset pain in the right knee. He describes it as incredibly intense; he has not had any previous episodes. After examination of the knee, joint fluid is aspirated and sent to the lab. The rheumatology team are suspecting a diagnosis of pseudogout. Which of the following features would aid in distinguishing this from gout?
options: Warmth at the site of pain
explanation:
Chondrocalcinosis
Chondrocalcinosis helps to distinguish pseudogout from gout. This can be seen as linear calcifications of the meniscus and articular cartilage on an x-ray of the knee. This is seen in pseudogout, but not particularly associated with gout, and so it can be used to distinguish between the two.

Age
Age is not a particularly distinguishing factor between gout and pseudogout. This patient is 64 years old; this does not sway the diagnosis one way or the other.

Presence of crystals
Simply the presence of crystals is not a distinguishing factor - they are present in both conditions. The type of crystals, however, differs between the two. Pseudogout crystals are weakly-positively birefringent rhomboid-shaped. Gout crystals are negatively birefringent.

Response to colchicine
Both conditions usually respond well to colchicine with regards to acute pain management, and so this is not a distinguishing factor.

Warmth at the site of pain
There may be increased warmth of the affected joint in both conditions and so this is not a useful factor to distinguish between the two.

stem: A 25-year-old presents with repeated episodes of severe muscle cramping and dark-coloured urine following short bouts of intense exercise. He reports that his symptoms improve with rest but recur with similar exertion. There is no significant family history, and he denies the use of steroids or other performance-enhancing drugs. Blood and urine: 138 g/L (135-175) WCC 6.5 x10⁹/L (4.0-11.0) Plat 240 x10⁹/L (150-450) CK 25,000 U/L (< 200) Myoglobin (serum) 1,000 µg/L (< 70) Urea 7.5 mmol/L (2.5-7.8) Cr 110 µmol/L (60-110) Urine myoglobin Positive Negative Urine dipstick Blood 3+ Negative Hb What is the mechanism of the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Myophosphorylase deficiency
Repeated cramping, rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria after short bouts of exercise can point towards McArdle's disease. This patient’s history of repeated cramping, rhabdomyolysis, and myoglobinuria after short bouts of exercise strongly suggests McArdle's disease, a glycogen storage disorder. The presentation, including marked elevations in CK and serum myoglobin, aligns with impaired energy metabolism in skeletal muscle. McArdle's disease is caused by myophosphorylase deficiency, an enzyme critical for glycogen breakdown in muscle cells. Without functional myophosphorylase, muscles cannot effectively utilise glycogen as a rapid energy source during exertion, leading to muscle breakdown and the characteristic symptoms. The disorder's hallmark is exercise intolerance during short, intense activity, as seen in this case. The presence of urine myoglobin further indicates muscle injury. Recognising these symptoms and the associated enzymatic deficiency is essential for diagnosing McArdle’s disease and differentiating it from other metabolic myopathies.

Acid maltase deficiency
Acid maltase deficiency is incorrect because it leads to glycogen accumulation in lysosomes, causing Pompe disease. This condition typically presents with progressive muscle weakness, respiratory insufficiency, and cardiomyopathy rather than acute exercise-induced rhabdomyolysis. Symptoms do not resolve with rest and are unrelated to short-term glycogen mobilisation failures, as seen in McArdle’s disease.

Aldolase A deficiency
Aldolase A deficiency is incorrect because this glycolytic enzyme deficiency impairs energy production in both skeletal muscle and erythrocytes. While patients may experience muscle cramps during exercise, they also present with chronic haemolytic anaemia, a finding absent in this case. Additionally, Aldolase A deficiency is not associated with the classic features of rhabdomyolysis or myoglobinuria following short, intense exercise bouts.

Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency is incorrect as it is a disorder of fatty acid oxidation. Symptoms occur after prolonged fasting or sustained exercise when fat metabolism becomes the primary energy source. Unlike McArdle’s disease, episodes are triggered by long-term energy demands, not short, high-intensity efforts, and rhabdomyolysis is associated with prolonged exercise or metabolic stress.

Phosphofructokinase deficiency
Phosphofructokinase deficiency is incorrect as it causes Tarui disease, another glycolytic pathway disorder. It results in muscle pain, fatigue, and exercise intolerance during sustained, submaximal activity. Haemolysis is also a feature due to red blood cell involvement. The clinical pattern differs from McArdle’s disease, which is triggered by brief, high-intensity exercise and does not involve haemolytic anaemia.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with muscle aches presents to the general practice. She has been experiencing this for well over a year and it affects her chest and back more so than her limbs. On questioning, she alludes to having bouts on average every 3 months of becoming short of breath. She lives a very healthy lifestyle remaining abstinent from drinking and smoking. On examination, she has a flat erythematous rash on her torso and purple discolouration bilaterally around the eyelids which she explains she has had for a long time. Which antibody is associated with the patient's condition?
explanation:
Anti-Jo-1
Dermatomyositis is associated with the anti-Jo-1 antibody. Dermatomyositis is a rare inflammatory muscle disease comprised of muscle weakness, muscle pains, and a skin rash. The weakness tends to be proximal and can affect the patient's breathing. In addition to this, systemic symptoms can occur, some include arrhythmias, dysphagia, joint calcifications. A high yield point to remember is the association of the heliotrope rash and dermatomyositis which is described as the purple discolouration in the question vignette. Multiple antibodies are associated with dermatomyositis including ANA (antinuclear antibody), anti M2, and anti-Jo1. All these vary in sensitivity and specificity. It is important to note that anti-Jo-1 is more sensitive for polymyositis but is also found in dermatomyositis.

Anti-Scl-70
Anti-Scl-70 is a type of anti-nuclear antibody which is found in scleroderma.

Anti-smooth muscle
Anti-smooth muscle antibody is associated with autoimmune hepatitis.

Anti-histone
Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus.

C-ANCA
C-ANCA stands for C anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody and is associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (previously known as Wegener's granulomatosis).

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology clinic for review. She reports a six-month history of arthralgia and swelling affecting the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints of both hands. On examination, she has boggy swelling of the third, fourth and fifth MCP joints bilaterally, with erythema and mild tenderness to palpation. No gross deformities are noted in either hand, and she has a normal range of motion and motor function bilaterally. Investigation results are shown below: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibody titre 48U (<20) What is the most likely hand X-ray findings for this patient?
explanation:
Juxta-articular osteopaenia
Juxta-articular osteoporosis/osteopenia is an early x-ray feature of rheumatoid arthritis. The correct answer is juxta-articular osteopaenia. This patient has a likely new diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. This is based on the symmetrical arthropathy affecting multiple joints in her hands, with a positive anti-CCP titre. Juxta-articular osteopenia is a common early Xray feature of rheumatoid arthritis and is the most likely finding in this clinical scenario.

Joint subluxation
Joint subluxation is incorrect. Although this can be seen in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, it would be unlikely to be present on an initial X-ray at the point of diagnosis, and usually occurs in the context of progressive disease. In addition, the clinical examination findings do not suggest the presence of joint subluxation.

Peri-articular erosions
Peri-articular erosions is incorrect. These would also be seen in the context of progressive rheumatoid arthritis, and are not classically seen on initial diagnostic X-rays.

Subchondral cysts
Subchondral cysts is incorrect. These tend to be seen on the X-rays of patients with osteoarthritis rather than rheumatoid arthritis.

Subchondral sclerosis
Subchondral sclerosis is incorrect. These are also X-ray findings suggestive of osteoarthritis rather than rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A 48-year-old man is seen in the transplant follow-up clinic. He had a heart transplant last month and is now taking tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisolone as his immunosuppression. Due to the ongoing need for steroids, a DEXA scan is arranged for the patient, the results of which are shown below: Region T-score Z-score Lumbar spine -0.7 -0.5 Femoral neck -1.2 -0.9 What is the most accurate interpretation of these results?
options: This patient has normal bone density for his age, gender and ethnicity
This patient has osteoporosis of the femoral neck but normal bone density of the lumbar spine
This patient's bone density is greater than expected for his age, gender and ethnicity
explanation:
This patient has osteopenia
This patient has osteopenia is correct. This patient has a T-score of less than -1 for his femoral neck measurement, suggesting osteopenia. Osteopenia or osteoporosis detected in one measurement site means there is generalised osteopenia or osteoporosis; it is a systemic process and cannot be localised to only one region. The T-score is a measure of the bone mineral density compared to a healthy young adult. The T-score can be used to diagnose osteoporosis (if less than -2.5), or osteopenia (if between -1 and -2.5).

This patient has normal bone density for his age, gender and ethnicity
This patient has normal bone density for his age, gender, and ethnicity is incorrect. This patient has a T-score of less than -1 for his femoral neck measurement, suggesting osteopenia.

This patient has osteoporosis
This patient has osteoporosis is incorrect. Osteoporosis is diagnosed by a T-score of less than -2.5 at any measurement site, or suggested by a Z-score of less than -2 (coupled with a suggestive history of fractures) in males under 50 or pre-menopausal women.

This patient has osteoporosis of the femoral neck but normal bone density of the lumbar spine
This patient has osteoporosis of the femoral neck but normal bone density of the lumbar spine is incorrect. This patient has a T-score of between -1 and -2.5 for his femoral neck measurement, suggesting osteopenia rather than osteoporosis. Osteopenia or osteoporosis detected in one measurement site means there is generalised osteopenia or osteoporosis; it is a systemic process and cannot be localised to only one region.

This patient's bone density is greater than expected for his age, gender and ethnicity
This patient's bone density is greater than expected for his age, gender, and ethnicity is incorrect. The negative values indicate that this patient's measurements are below the expected range. The T-score of less than -1 in the femoral neck is abnormal, indicating osteopenia.

stem: Which one of the following drugs has been associated with an increased risk of atypical stress fractures of the proximal femoral shaft?
explanation:
Alendronate
Alendronate is a bisphosphonate drug used in the treatment of osteoporosis and Paget's disease. It works by inhibiting osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, leading to an overall increase in total bone mass. However, long-term use of alendronate has been associated with atypical femoral fractures. These are stress or insufficiency fractures that occur in the subtrochanteric region or the shaft of the femur and are often bilateral. The mechanism behind this association is not fully understood but it is believed that suppression of bone turnover might lead to accumulation of microdamage within the bone, reducing its overall strength.

Spironolactone
Spironolactone, on the other hand, is a potassium-sparing diuretic used primarily to treat heart failure, liver cirrhosis, primary hyperaldosteronism and Conn's syndrome. Although it can cause gynaecomastia due to its anti-androgen effects, spironolactone has not been associated with an increased risk for atypical stress fractures.

Quetiapine
Quetiapine is an atypical antipsychotic medication used in the management of schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder. Its side effect profile includes weight gain, sedation and orthostatic hypotension but it does not increase the risk for atypical stress fractures.

Venlafaxine
Venlafaxine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI), is used primarily for depression and anxiety disorders. While venlafaxine may cause side effects such as nausea, dizziness and hypertension among others, there have been no reports linking it with an increased risk for atypical stress fractures.

Clopidogrel
Finally, Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet agent used to prevent blood clots after a recent heart attack or stroke, and in people with certain disorders of the heart or blood vessels. Its most common side effects include bleeding and bruising but it does not predispose patients to atypical stress fractures.

stem: A 39-year-old man is referred to orthopaedics with a 24-hour history of knee pain. He undergoes aspiration and urgent gram stain shows no organisms or crystals but many white blood cells. You are asked for a medical opinion. When you review the patient you note chemosis and watery discharge of both eyes and he reports dysuria for several days. He reports he is sexually active with one partner and they always use condoms. On further questioning, he reveals he had an episode of diarrhoea 3 weeks previously which resolved after 4 days. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Administer IM benzathine penicillin and refer to sexual health services
Start non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and refer to rheumatology
Take blood cultures and start IV flucloxacillin
explanation:
Start non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and refer to rheumatology
This patient has the classic triad of reactive arthritis (formerly known as Reiter's syndrome) - arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis. The recent episode of diarrhoea may have represented Campylobacter or Salmonella infection, which are common triggers for this condition. The correct answer is start non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and refer to rheumatology.

Administer IM benzathine penicillin and refer to sexual health services
Administer IM benzathine penicillin and refer to sexual health services is incorrect. This would be a treatment option for syphilis, which can present with synovitis. However, it usually presents with migratory polyarthritis rather than the monoarthritis described here. It would also not explain urethritis or recent diarrhoeal illness.

Organise joint washout
Organise joint washout is incorrect. This would be recommended in cases of septic arthritis in conjunction with appropriate IV antibiotics. However, the negative gram stain in the absence of recent antibiotic exposure makes septic arthritis unlikely here and invasive management would be inappropriate without good evidence of the diagnosis.

Start IV ceftriaxone
Start IV ceftriaxone is incorrect. This would be the treatment of choice for gonococcal arthritis. This can present with monoarthritis and a negative gram stain, but more commonly is seen in the context of disseminated gonococcal infection - this presents with dermatitis, polyarthritis and tenosynovitis. His sexual history also does not imply a high risk of this. It would also be unlikely to explain the recent diarrhoeal illness.

Take blood cultures and start IV flucloxacillin
Take blood cultures and start IV flucloxacillin is incorrect. This would be appropriate for septic arthritis, with the most common organisms being Staphylococcus aureus and beta-haemolytic streptococci. However, it is unusual to have a negative gram stain in such cases in the absence of recent antibiotic therapy. This would also not explain the ocular or urethral symptoms or the recent diarrhoeal illness.

stem: Which one of the following features is least commonly seen in patients with pseudoxanthoma elasticum?
options: Increased risk of ischaemic heart disease
explanation:
Retinitis pigmentosa
The correct answer is Retinitis pigmentosa. Pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE) is a rare genetic disorder that affects the connective tissues and is characterised by the calcification of elastic fibres. Retinitis pigmentosa, however, is not a typical feature of PXE. Instead, it's most commonly associated with other inherited retinal diseases.

Increased risk of ischaemic heart disease
Increased risk of ischaemic heart disease - This option is incorrect as PXE does indeed increase the risk of ischaemic heart disease. The condition leads to mineralisation and fragmentation of elastic fibres in blood vessels, which can cause narrowing or blockage of arteries leading to an increased risk for cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction.

Gastrointestinal haemorrhage
Gastrointestinal haemorrhage - Gastrointestinal haemorrhage is another common feature seen in patients with PXE. The same process that causes damage to blood vessels in the heart also affects vessels in the gastrointestinal tract, making this option incorrect.

Autosomal recessive inheritance
Autosomal recessive inheritance - PXE follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. Mutations in the ABCC6 gene are responsible for this condition. Therefore, both parents must carry one copy of the mutated gene to pass on this disorder to their child, making this option incorrect as well.

'Plucked chicken skin' appearance
'Plucked chicken skin' appearance - 'Plucked chicken skin' appearance refers to small yellowish papules often found on the neck and flexural areas in patients with PXE. It's one of the characteristic clinical features used for diagnosis, hence this option too is incorrect.

stem: A 33-year-old woman presents with back pain which radiates down her right leg. This came on suddenly when she was bending down to pick up her child. On examination straight leg raising is limited to 30 degrees on the right hand side due to shooting pains down her leg. Sensation is reduced on the dorsum of the right foot, particularly around the big toe and foot dorsiflexion is also weak. The ankle and knee reflexes appear intact. A diagnosis of disc prolapse is suspected. Which nerve root is most likely to be affected?
explanation:
L5
The patient's presentation of sudden onset back pain radiating down the leg, reduced straight leg raising test, and sensory and motor deficits are consistent with a lumbar disc prolapse. The L5 nerve root is most likely affected in this case due to the specific findings of reduced sensation on the dorsum of the right foot, particularly around the big toe, and weakness in foot dorsiflexion. These symptoms correspond to the dermatome and myotome supplied by the L5 nerve root.

L2
L2 nerve root involvement would typically present with weakness in hip flexion and pain or numbness in the anterior thigh region. This does not match the patient's symptoms.

L3
L3 nerve root compression would manifest as weakness in knee extension and difficulty walking up stairs or inclines. Sensory changes would be expected over the medial aspect of the knee. Again, these findings do not align with our patient's presentation.

L4
L4 nerve root impingement can cause weakness in ankle dorsiflexion; however, it would also present with decreased patellar reflexes and sensory changes overlying the medial malleolus or medial calf area. In this case, ankle reflexes were intact, making L4 less likely.

S1
S1 nerve root compression may result in pain radiating down to the posterior thigh and calf region along with weakness in plantar flexion of the foot. Additionally, patients may experience a loss of Achilles tendon reflex and sensory changes overlying the lateral foot or heel area. As these features do not match our patient's presentation, S1 involvement is less likely as well.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is referred to the dermatology clinic with a 6month history of progressive hair loss. On examination of her scalp, there are several well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with adherent scale and follicular plugging. The centre of the larger plaques appears atrophic with a loss of follicular openings. A smaller, similar-looking lesion is noted on the conchal bowl of her left ear. Systemic review is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Discoid lupus erythematosus
Discoid lupus erythematosus is the correct diagnosis. This patient presents with features highly characteristic of a primary scarring alopecia, specifically discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE). The key clinical signs are the well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with adherent scale and follicular plugging. The presence of central atrophy and loss of follicular openings confirms the scarring nature of the process, which results in permanent hair loss. DLE is the most common form of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus and frequently affects sun-exposed areas. The scalp is a common site, and the additional lesion on the conchal bowl of the ear is a classic finding that strongly supports this diagnosis. DLE is an autoimmune condition, and while it is a subtype of lupus, progression to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is uncommon (less than 5% of cases), which is consistent with the patient's unremarkable systemic review. Diagnosis is typically confirmed with a skin biopsy for histology and direct immunofluorescence.

Alopecia areata
Alopecia areata is a common cause of hair loss but is incorrect here. It is a non-scarring alopecia, meaning the hair follicles are preserved, and regrowth is possible. The typical presentation is one or more well-defined, completely smooth, circular patches of hair loss. There is no associated erythema, scaling, or atrophy as described in this case. The presence of scarring features, such as atrophy and loss of follicular openings, definitively rules out alopecia areata.

Lichen planopilaris
Lichen planopilaris is an important differential diagnosis as it is also a primary lymphocytic scarring alopecia. However, the clinical features are subtly different. Lichen planopilaris typically presents with perifollicular erythema and scaling (keratotic plugs at the edge of the hair follicle), rather than the larger, disc-like erythematous plaques with central atrophy seen in DLE. While it leads to scarring alopecia with loss of follicular openings, the overall morphology described in the scenario, particularly the 'discoid' nature of the plaques and the involvement of the ear, makes DLE a more likely diagnosis.

Tinea capitis
Tinea capitis is a fungal infection of the scalp and is less likely in this scenario. While it can cause hair loss and scaling, it is more common in children. The appearance is typically of scaly patches with broken-off hairs ('black dots'). An inflammatory form, known as a kerion, can present as a boggy, pustular mass and may lead to scarring, but this does not match the description of atrophic, erythematous plaques with follicular plugging. The presentation in this adult patient is not typical for tinea capitis.

Androgenetic alopecia
Androgenetic alopecia, or pattern hair loss, is the most common cause of hair loss but is incorrect. It is a non-scarring, non-inflammatory process. In women, it typically presents as diffuse thinning over the central scalp, with preservation of the frontal hairline (a 'Christmas tree' pattern). It does not cause the discrete, inflamed, scaly, and atrophic plaques described in the clinical scenario.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of a swollen, painful left knee. Aspirated joint fluid shows calcium pyrophosphate crystals. Which of the following blood tests is most useful in revealing an underlying cause?
explanation:
Transferrin saturation
Haemochromatosis is a risk factor for pseudogout. This is a typical presentation of pseudogout. An elevated transferrin saturation may indicate haemochromatosis, a recognised cause of pseudogout.

Serum ferritin
A high ferritin level is also seen in haemochromatosis but can be raised in a variety of infective and inflammatory processes, including pseudogout, as part of an acute phase response.

stem: Which one of the following features is least typical of polymyalgia rheumatica?
options: Morning stiffness in proximal limb muscles
explanation:
Elevated creatine kinase
The correct answer is Elevated creatine kinase. Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is an inflammatory condition that typically presents with aching and stiffness in the proximal muscles of the shoulder and hip girdle, often associated with symptoms such as low-grade fever, anorexia, malaise and weight loss. However, PMR does not typically cause muscle damage or myopathy, which would be suggested by elevated levels of creatine kinase (CK). CK is a muscle enzyme that leaks out of damaged or inflamed muscle cells, therefore its elevation indicates muscle inflammation or injury rather than PMR.

Low-grade fever
Low-grade fever can be a symptom of PMR. It's caused by systemic inflammation that also results in the characteristic musculoskeletal symptoms. This inflammation can stimulate the hypothalamus to increase body temperature.

Morning stiffness in proximal limb muscles
Morning stiffness in proximal limb muscles is one of the hallmark features of PMR. It's caused by inflammation in these areas which gets worse after periods of inactivity like sleeping overnight.

Polyarthralgia
Polyarthralgia, meaning pain in multiple joints, can also occur in PMR due to widespread inflammation. However, it's important to note that this is distinct from true arthritis - there's no joint destruction or deformity seen on imaging studies in patients with PMR.

Anorexia
Anorexia can also be seen in patients with PMR. This might be due to systemic inflammation causing general feelings of being unwell and reducing appetite. Alternatively, it could be related to other associated conditions such as giant cell arteritis which may cause jaw claudication leading to difficulties eating.

stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with painful joints. She says the joints in her hands are becoming stiff, swollen, and painful. The stiffness is worse in the mornings. On examination, some of the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands are swollen. They are tender to palpate and there is a reduced range of movement in the fingers. Relevant bloods are shown below: Hb 110 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 456 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 10.6 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) CRP 34 mg/L (< 5) Rheumatoid factor Positive Anti-CCP Positive Given the most likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate management?
options: Dual DMARD therapy with bridging steroids
Single DMARD therapy with bridging steroids
TNF-α inhibitor and single DMARD combination therapy
explanation:
Single DMARD therapy with bridging steroids
Single DMARD therapy with bridging steroids is correct. This patient's signs, symptoms, and blood results suggest a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. The current recommendation is that early DMARD monotherapy should be used, usually with steroids to control symptoms whilst the DMARD is initiated, as steroids act faster than the DMARDs.

Dual DMARD therapy with bridging steroids
Dual DMARD therapy with bridging steroids is incorrect. This patient's signs, symptoms, and blood results suggest a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. The current evidence suggests that early DMARD monotherapy should be used, usually with steroids to control symptoms whilst the DMARD is initiated. Combination therapy may be used if the patient has not responded to monotherapy at 3 months.

High dose oral tapering steroids
High dose oral tapering steroids is incorrect. In rheumatoid arthritis, steroids are used either as bridging to reduce symptoms whilst the DMARD is initiated or as treatment of acute flares. Management of a new diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis does not consist of steroids alone, and bridging doses used are generally low (less than 10mg prednisolone per day). This answer is therefore incorrect.

Paracetamol and topical NSAIDs
Paracetamol and topical NSAIDs is incorrect. This is the first-line treatment for osteoarthritis, particularly in the hands or knees. The patient in this case, however, is suffering from rheumatoid arthritis. The early morning stiffness, proximal interphalangeal joint/metacarpophalangeal joint involvement, and blood results suggest rheumatoid arthritis rather than osteoarthritis.

TNF-α inhibitor and single DMARD combination therapy
TNF-α inhibitor and single DMARD combination therapy is incorrect. TNF-α inhibitors may be used in rheumatoid arthritis if the patient does not respond to the DMARD monotherapy within 3 months.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents with a spontaneous pneumothorax. He is noted to be of slim build with a tall stature and a high arched palate. His family who attends the hospital with him have a similar appearance. You suspect Marfan's syndrome. This disease is caused by a mutation in the gene that encodes which protein?
explanation:
Fibrillin-1
Marfan's syndrome is caused by a mutation in a protein called fibrillin-1. Mutation of FBN1 that encodes Fibrillin-1 is responsible for Marfan's syndrome.

stem: A 55-year-old right-handed male cleaner presents with elbow pain. He describes a gradual onset of pain in his right elbow over a period of six weeks with only mild relief from paracetamol. The patient plays golf and exercises at the gym weekly. He does remember a fall at work six weeks ago where he fell onto his left elbow. The patient feels systemically well and denies any pyrexia. On examination, the patient describes tenderness over the right elbow with resisted wrist extension/supination and the elbow held in extension. There is no significant swelling over the olecranon. What is the most likely cause of this man's elbow pain?
explanation:
Lateral epicondylitis
Lateral epicondylitis: worse on resisted wrist extension/suppination whilst elbow extended. The most likely answer here is lateral epicondylitis. Lateral epicondylitis or 'tennis elbow' presents with gradual onset pain around the lateral epicondyle of the humerus radiating to the forearm. This patient's job is a cleaner, therefore undertaking repetitive movements with his dominant hand increases the chance of lateral epicondylitis.

Medial epicondylitis
Medial epicondylitis or 'golfer's elbow' presents with pain around the medial epicondyle. Pain is elicited during wrist flexion and pronation and does not match the examination findings in the scenario.

Olecranon bursitis
Olecranon bursitis presents with swelling and erythema over the olecranon, this patient does not have this as outlined in the question.

Radial head fracture
Radial head fractures present with immediate pain and swelling, the patient in this case presented with gradual onset pain; making a fracture a less likely differential in this patient.

Septic arthritis
As this patient is systemically well, septic arthritis is unlikely. Also, the affected joint will appear red, painful and swollen.

stem: A 24-year-old female is investigated for intermittent pain and swelling of the metacarpal phalangeal joints for the past 3 months. An x-ray shows loss of joint space and soft-tissue swelling. Rheumatoid factor is positive and a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis is made. What is the most appropriate management to slow disease progression?
explanation:
Methotrexate + short-course of prednisolone
In 2018 NICE updated their rheumatoid arthritis guidelines. They now recommend disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) monotherapy with a short-course of bridging prednisolone.

stem: A 53-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of bilateral hand and wrist pain, with accompanying swelling of the fingers. She describes morning stiffness that lasts for several hours, and the pain is increasingly affecting her daily functioning. She has no significant past medical history. On examination, several small joints of the hands are swollen and tender. The patient is referred for blood tests: CRP 58 mg/L Anti-CCP antibodies Positive (< 5) She is then referred for hand X-rays, the results of which are awaited. What finding is most supportive of the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Periarticular erosions
Periarticular erosions on x-ray are suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis. This patient's presentation is suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), as suggested by the bilateral polyarthritis of small joints, prolonged morning stiffness, raised CRP and the presence of anti-CCP antibodies. Of the X-ray findings listed here, periarticular erosions are the most supportive of the diagnosis of RA.

Loss of joint space
Loss of joint space is incorrect. Although this may be seen in RA, it is not specific to the condition as it is also a common finding in osteoarthritis (OA).

Osteophytes
Osteophytes is incorrect. These are commonly associated with findings of OA on X-ray, rather than RA.

Subchondral cysts
Subchondral cysts is incorrect. These are typically associated with OA, rather than RA.

Subchondral sclerosis
Subchondral sclerosis is incorrect. This is usually associated with OA, not RA.

stem: A 60-year-old man with a past medical history of osteoarthritis presents with a swollen, red and hot left knee joint. He is unable to move it due to the pain. On examination he is pyrexial with a temperature of 38.7 C and a blood sample shows a white cell count of 22.8 *109/l. Following joint aspiration, what is the most appropriate antibiotic therapy?
explanation:
IV flucloxacillin
IV flucloxacillin is the correct first-line treatment for suspected septic arthritis in this case. The most common causative organism in native joint septic arthritis is Staphylococcus aureus, and flucloxacillin provides excellent coverage against methicillin-sensitive S. aureus (MSSA). The clinical presentation of acute onset monoarthritis with fever, raised inflammatory markers, and inability to move the joint is highly suggestive of septic arthritis. In the UK, empirical treatment with IV flucloxacillin alone is appropriate unless there are specific risk factors for methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) or other organisms.

IV flucloxacillin + benzylpenicillin
IV flucloxacillin + benzylpenicillin combination provides unnecessarily broad coverage. While benzylpenicillin would cover streptococci, these are much less common causes of native joint septic arthritis in adults, and flucloxacillin alone provides adequate coverage for most streptococci.

IV gentamicin + benzylpenicillin
IV gentamicin + benzylpenicillin is not appropriate as first-line therapy as it does not provide optimal coverage against S. aureus. This combination would be more suitable for suspected gonococcal arthritis in younger patients with appropriate risk factors.

IV vancomycin + cefotaxime
IV vancomycin + cefotaxime is too broad-spectrum for initial therapy in this case. Vancomycin would only be indicated if there were risk factors for MRSA, while cefotaxime provides unnecessarily broad gram-negative coverage.

IV gentamicin + rifampicin + benzylpenicillin
IV gentamicin + rifampicin + benzylpenicillin is an overly complex regimen that would typically be reserved for prosthetic joint infections or cases where standard therapy has failed. This triple therapy is not appropriate as first-line treatment for native joint septic arthritis.

stem: A 54-year-old male presents with weakness of his upper arms. On examination he is found to have a macular rash over his back and the extensor aspects of his upper arms. He is a heavy smoker and his sodium is 121 mmol/l. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Dermatomyositis
This man may have an underlying small cell lung cancer causing Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion. However, the presence of a macular rash over his back and the extensor aspects of his upper arms, along with muscle weakness, is most consistent with dermatomyositis.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents following a recurred episode of back pain. The patient has had multiple issues following a disc prolapse sustained during his career working in manual labour. The patient reports today he was bending over to pick something up and had an acute onset of lower back pain. On exam, he had a unilateral, decreased sensation on the posterolateral aspect of the right leg and lateral foot. A straight leg raise test results in pain in the thigh, buttock and calf region and there is weakness on plantar flexion with reduced ankle reflexes. What root compression has this patient experienced?
explanation:
S1 nerve root compression
S1 lesion features = Sensory loss of posterolateral aspect of leg and lateral aspect of foot, weakness in plantar flexion of foot, reduced ankle reflex, positive sciatic nerve stretch test. This patient has presented with a prolapsed spinal disc producing an S1 nerve root compression. Disc prolapses normal produce a clear dermatomal pain pattern and neurological deficit due to a single nerve root being compressed. As seen in this case compression of the S1 nerve root results in a sensory loss of the posterolateral aspect of the leg and lateral aspect of the foot. There is a weakness of foot plantar flexion and ankle reflexes are normally reduced. Finally, pain can be elicited when the patient performs a straight leg raise; known as the sciatic nerve stretch test.

L1-2 nerve root compression
An L1-2 nerve root compression will result in discomfort over the groin and upper thigh region with associated weakness of the pelvic and psoas muscles. Although rare, patients suffering prolapse of the L1-2 discs often have difficulty lifting the affected leg and therefore struggle to walk upstairs etc.

L3 nerve root compression
The pain pattern and neurological deficit of an L3 nerve root compression is commonly a sensory loss over the anterior aspect of the thigh, weakness of the quadriceps with a reduction in the knee reflex on the affected side. Finally, pain can be elicited in the anterior thigh when performing the femoral stretch test, where the knee is passively flexed with the patient lying prone.

L4 nerve root compression
An L4 nerve root compression can present with a very similar pattern to an L3 compression with weakness of the quadriceps, a reduced knee reflex and a positive femoral stretch test. In L4 root compression, however, there will be a sensory loss over the anterior aspect of the knee, not the thigh.

L5 nerve root compression
L5 nerve root compression can be identified on examination by evidence of sensory loss on the dorsum aspect of the foot with weakness of the foot and big toe dorsiflexion. L5 nerve compressions will also result in a positive sciatic nerve stretch test but the reflexes are normally unaffected.

stem: What is the most common target of pANCA?
explanation:
Myeloperoxidase
The major target for pANCA is myeloperoxidase (MPO). Myeloperoxidase is a neutrophil protein whose primary role is the generation of oxygen free radicals.

stem: A 62-year-old man is reviewed on the acute medical ward with a two week history of lumbar back pain and fevers. He complains of point tenderness over the L1-2 area and finds it difficult to mobilise. You arrange for an MRI of his lumbar spine which is reported as follows: 'Area of hyperintensity visible at the L1-2 disc space with vertebral end plate changes suggestive of vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis.' Which of the following organisms is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of osteomyelitis. In the majority of cases, osteomyelitis and discitis is caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

Streptococcus pyogenes
The other organisms are all capable of causing osteomyelitis and discitis however disease caused by these organisms occurs much less commonly than that caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

Salmonella enterica
In patients with sickle cell anaemia and other haemoglobinopathies, Salmonella sp. become more common however it is usually preceded by a period of gastrointestinal upset.

Escherichia coli
The other organisms are all capable of causing osteomyelitis and discitis however disease caused by these organisms occurs much less commonly than that caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa
The other organisms are all capable of causing osteomyelitis and discitis however disease caused by these organisms occurs much less commonly than that caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

stem: A 45-year-old female with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents to the Emergency Department with a two day history of a hot, painful, swollen right elbow joint. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Joint aspiration
