Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect - this would usually lead to symmetrical polyarthritis of several small joints, usually affecting metacarpophalangeal joints but sparing the DIPs. Morning stiffness would typically be much more prolonged than the few minutes mentioned in this scenario.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents to the emergency department with reduced mobility. He describes finding it difficult to walk due to weakness in his left foot. There is no past medical history of note and he is normally fit and well and is a regular sports player. On examination, there is reduced sensation in the lateral aspect of the left foot and posterior aspect of the left leg. He has normal power on dorsiflexion but reduced power on plantarflexion of his left foot. Ankle reflexes are lost. Damage to what anatomical structure is likely to cause the patient's presentation?
explanation:
S1 nerve root
S1 lesion features = Sensory loss of posterolateral aspect of leg and lateral aspect of foot, weakness in plantar flexion of foot, reduced ankle reflex, positive sciatic nerve stretch test. S1 nerve root is correct. This patient has features of S1 nerve root impingement. The S1 nerve supplies sensation to the posterolateral aspect of the leg and lateral aspect of the foot. A lesion in the nerve also gives rise to a loss or weakness in the ankle reflex and weakness in plantarflexion.

Achilles tendon
Achilles tendon is incorrect. An Achilles tendon rupture presents as a painful 'pop' sensation at the back of the heel. A positive Simmonds-Thompson test is seen where squeezing the calf muscle fails to cause plantarflexion of the foot. It would not account for the sensory loss seen in this patient.

Common fibular nerve
Common fibular nerve is incorrect. Injury to the common fibular nerve commonly occurs following injury to the neck of the fibular. It causes 'foot drop' and loss of dorsiflexion of the foot. This is not what is seen in this patient.

L4-L5 nerve roots
L4-L5 nerve root is incorrect. The L4-L5 nerve roots supply sensation to the anterior knee and dorsum of the foot, respectively. Lesions or compression of these nerve roots causes weakness in the quadriceps and dorsiflexion of the foot and big toe.

Sural nerve
Sural nerve is incorrect. The sural nerve is a sensory nerve that supplies the lower posterolateral leg and lateral foot. Whilst the pattern of sensory loss is similar in this patient, the sural nerve carries no motor fibres and would not account for the weakness in plantarflexion, making an S1 nerve root injury more likely.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with sudden onset severe pain, redness, and swelling in his right big toe, which started overnight. He has a history of hypertension and obesity but no previous similar episodes. Examination reveals erythema, warmth, and tenderness over the first metatarsophalangeal joint. The joint aspiration shows negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals under polarised light microscopy. Which is the most appropriate long-term management strategy for this patient?
options: Advise lifestyle modifications only and reassess if symptoms recur
Prescribing allopurinol after the acute attack has resolved
Prescribing colchicine daily for long-term prophylaxis
Starting allopurinol immediately alongside treatment for the acute attack
Use NSAIDs intermittently for future flare-ups without uratelowering therapy
explanation:
Prescribing allopurinol after the acute attack has resolved
Prescribing allopurinol after the acute attack has resolved is correct because current guidelines recommend offering urate-lowering therapy (ULT) to all patients after their first attack of gout, regardless of symptom recurrence, to prevent future flares and long-term joint damage. Allopurinol (a xanthine oxidase inhibitor) is the first-line ULT and should be started after the acute attack has fully resolved, as initiating it during an active flare may worsen or prolong the attack. The crystal-confirmed gout makes allopurinol the most appropriate long-term management option.

Advise lifestyle modifications only and reassess if symptoms recur
Advise lifestyle modifications only and reassess if symptoms recur is incorrect because while lifestyle modifications (e.g., weight loss, reducing alcohol and purine intake, staying hydrated) are beneficial, they are not sufficient alone to prevent future gout attacks. Allopurinol should be initiated after the first gout attack, as many patients will have recurrent attacks, and untreated hyperuricemia increases the risk of chronic gouty arthritis and tophi formation.

Prescribing colchicine daily for long-term prophylaxis
Prescribing colchicine daily for long-term prophylaxis is incorrect because although low-dose colchicine can be used for short-term prophylaxis (6 months) when starting urate-lowering therapy, it is not a substitute for allopurinol in the long-term management of gout. Colchicine helps reduce acute flare-ups but does not lower uric acid levels or prevent joint damage.

Starting allopurinol immediately alongside treatment for the acute attack
Starting allopurinol immediately alongside treatment for the acute attack is incorrect because initiating allopurinol during an active gout attack can trigger or prolong the flare due to fluctuations in uric acid levels. The best approach is to first control the acute inflammation with NSAIDs, colchicine, or corticosteroids, then start allopurinol 2 weeks after symptom resolution to prevent further attacks.

Use NSAIDs intermittently for future flare-ups without uratelowering therapy
Use NSAIDs intermittently for future flare-ups without uratelowering therapy is incorrect because while NSAIDs are effective for acute gout management, they do not address the underlying hyperuricemia and do not prevent joint damage from recurrent attacks. Urate-lowering therapy should be offered after the first attack to reduce long-term complications.

stem: A 76-year-old man presents to his oncology follow-up appointment. Three years ago, he was diagnosed with poorly differentiated prostate cancer and a recent MRI of the spine revealed significant bone metastases. He is experiencing pain due to this and has trialled several analgesics without satisfactory results. He wishes to avoid radiotherapy because of its adverse effects. The attending physician proposes starting intravenous zoledronic acid for palliative management. What risk is significantly increased by this treatment in light of the patient's current condition?
explanation:
Osteonecrosis of the jaw
Osteonecrosis of the jaw is the correct answer. The patient presents with pain secondary to metastatic bone disease, against a background of prostate cancer. Metastatic bone pain is commonly managed with over-the-counter analgesics, opioids, and radiotherapy. Bisphosphonates may also be administered to limit damage to bone architecture caused by metastases, aid in the prevention of pathological fractures, and serve as an adjunct in pain control alongside other analgesics and radiotherapy. Intravenous (IV) bisphosphonates, particularly those used in cancer treatment, have been associated with a significantly increased risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw compared to oral bisphosphonates prescribed for conditions such as osteoporosis and Paget's disease. This increased risk is attributed to the action of bisphosphonates in inhibiting bone resorption by inducing osteoclast apoptosis and preventing their migration to the bone. The consequent limited formation of new bone allows the old bone to persist beyond its natural lifespan, with a compromised blood supply from dysfunctional capillary perfusion leading to avascular necrosis. The jawbone is particularly susceptible to osteonecrosis due to its higher rate of remodelling, rendering it more vulnerable to the effects of bisphosphonates. IV administration poses a greater risk than oral intake due to higher potency and has a more significant impact on patients with cancer because of the disease's effect on bone architecture.

Atypical stress fractures
Atypical stress fractures is incorrect. While there is an association between atypical stress fractures, particularly those affecting the proximal femoral shaft and bisphosphonate use, whether there is an increased risk among cancer patients receiving IV bisphosphonates remains undocumented or poorly understood. Moreover, atypical stress fractures are more commonly linked with alendronate use.

Hypocalcaemia
Hypocalcaemia is incorrect. Although bisphosphonates can cause hypocalcaemia, it rarely presents as a significant clinical problem in patients. Conversely, individuals with metastatic bone disease like our case are more susceptible to hypercalcaemia due to increased bone resorption from the underlying pathology.

Oesophageal ulcers
Oesophageal ulcers is incorrect as well; IV bisphosphonate therapy reduces the risk since it obviates the need for oral ingestion which could potentially irritate the oesophagus.

Oesophagitis
Oesophagitis is also incorrect. Oesophagitis constitutes a well-known adverse effect associated with oral bisphosphonate therapy necessitating stringent counselling for patients on such treatment; however, this issue does not hold similar significance in IV bisphosphate therapy.

stem: A 36-year-old patient presents with a facial rash and joint pains. She has a history of recurrent miscarriages and had a deep vein thrombosis at the age of 19. On examination, there is a butterfly-shaped rash on her cheeks that spares the nasolabial folds. Tenderness and swelling affect the small joints of her hands bilaterally. Her temperature is 37.8ºC. Given the likely diagnosis, what result best supports the presence of active disease?
explanation:
Low complement levels
SLE: complement levels (C3, C4) are usually low during active disease - may be used to monitor flares. Low complement levels is correct. This patient presents with a malar rash (butterfly rash that spares the nasolabial folds) and synovitis. Along with the history of recurrent miscarriage and previous venous thromboembolism, this suggests a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with secondary anti-phospholipid syndrome. Complement levels (C3 and C4) are typically low in active disease - that is, related to disease activity.

Low anti-double stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) antibodies
Low anti-dsDNA antibodies is incorrect. High anti-dsDNA antibody levels typically suggest active disease in SLE.

Polycythaemia
Polycythaemia is incorrect. Patients with SLE may be anaemic for a variety of causes such as anaemia of chronic disease, haemolytic anaemia or aplastic anaemia. Some of those states may be related to active disease. However, polycythaemia - raised haemoglobin - is not typically a feature of active SLE.

Positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA)
Positive ANA is incorrect. The ANA must be positive to obtain a diagnosis of SLE. However, it is not related to whether the disease is currently active.

Positive lupus anticoagulant
Positive lupus anticoagulant is incorrect. This may be positive in antiphospholipid syndrome and indeed this patient may have this diagnosis. However, it has no relation to whether the disease is active or not.

stem: A 45-year-old man who is known to have haemochromatosis presents with a swollen and painful right knee. An x-ray shows no fracture but extensive chondrocalcinosis. Given the likely diagnosis, which one of the following is most likely to present in the joint fluid?
explanation:
Positively birefringent rhomboid-shaped crystals
In a patient with haemochromatosis and chondrocalcinosis, the likely diagnosis is calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease or pseudogout. The characteristic finding in joint fluid analysis in CPPD disease is the presence of positively birefringent rhomboid-shaped crystals. These crystals are formed due to the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate in the joint cartilage, leading to inflammation and pain.

Raised hyaluronic acid levels
The first option, Raised hyaluronic acid levels, is not specific to any particular type of arthritis. Hyaluronic acid is a normal component of synovial fluid that provides lubrication and shock absorption. Its levels can be increased or decreased in various arthritic conditions but would not be diagnostic for CPPD disease.

Monosodium urate crystals
The second option, Monosodium urate crystals, are associated with gout rather than pseudogout. Gout is caused by the deposition of monosodium urate crystals within joints, leading to an inflammatory response and acute attacks of arthritis. Although both gout and pseudogout can present with similar symptoms, their underlying pathophysiology and crystal types are different.

Bipyramidal oxalate crystals
The third option, Bipyramidal oxalate crystals, are typically found in patients with primary hyperoxaluria or oxalosis, which results from excessive production or ingestion of oxalic acid. This condition can lead to kidney stones and systemic deposition of calcium oxalate crystals but would not cause chondrocalcinosis or pseudogout-like symptoms.

Negatively birefringent calcium carbonate crystals
The fourth option, Negatively birefringent calcium carbonate crystals, does not correspond to any known pathological process in joint diseases. Calcium carbonate crystals do not typically form in the joint space, and their presence would not be expected in a patient with haemochromatosis and chondrocalcinosis.

stem: An 18-year-old boy presented with sudden onset acute pain in the right hip for 9-days. The pain, associated with high-grade fever with chills, was non-radiating, severe in intensity and aggravated by movements at the hip, and was only partly relieved with analgesia. The fever was remittent and was relieved with paracetamol but only to reoccur. He denies any history of trauma. What is the key investigation in this case given the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Synovial fluid analysis
Synovial fluid sampling is the key investigation in patients with suspected septic arthritis. Septic arthritis is an inflammatory joint condition secondary to joint inoculation with infectious microorganisms. Synovial fluid analysis is the key investigation in patients with suspected septic arthritis that includes culture and is the cornerstone of diagnosis and should be performed prior to antibiotic therapy being administered. It enables the diagnoses of both sepsis and crystal-induced arthritis to be confirmed quickly and therefore is the correct answer.

Blood culture
Blood cultures may help to identify the causative organism in cases where synovial fluid culture remains unrewarding. Whilst taking blood cultures is a necessary part of the septic screen, synovial fluid analysis remains fundamental.

Bone scan
Bone scans perform well for distinguishing sepsis from osteoarthrosis, but cannot distinguish effectively between sepsis and other causes of joint inflammation making its value limited in this case.

CT right hip
CT right hip similarly shows features found on radiographs however a fat-fluid level can be a specific sign in the absence of trauma. Bone scans perform well for distinguishing sepsis from osteoarthrosis, but cannot distinguish effectively between sepsis and other causes of joint inflammation making its value limited in this case.

Right hip x-ray
Right hip x-ray is unlikely to be useful in the acute stage of septic arthritis as it is likely to remain normal. It may show a narrowing of the joint space due to cartilage destruction or joint effusion. Therefore it is considered a key investigation.

stem: A 29-year-old with adult onset Still's comes to the rheumatology clinic for review. She still has significant symptoms including joint pains and a persistent skin rash despite methotrexate and etanercept. Examination reveals a macular erythematous rash and active synovitis. CRP is elevated at 95 mg/l. Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation:
Anakinra
The evidence is very strong to support the use of IL-1 inhibition for adult onset Still's disease. A review of published data estimated the overall remission rate at over 80%, and complete remission rate at approximately 66%. Anakinra competitively inhibits the action of IL-1 by binding to the IL-1 receptor and plasma levels correlate well with IL-1 in synovial fluid and presence of synovitis.

Denosumab
Denosumab is a RANK ligand inhibitor used in the treatment of osteoporosis.

Mepolizumab
Mepolizumab is used in the treatment of severe asthma with elevated eosinophils.

Rituximab
Rituximab is usually instigated in patients who fail to respond to anakinra.

Tocilizumab
There is some evidence to support the use of tocilizumab, an anti-IL6 monoclonal antibody in adult onset Still's, but there is stronger data to support a role for tocilizumab in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A 43-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with one week of joint pain and swelling. The pain and swelling are worst in the morning and improve over the course of the day and with activity. He has no past medical history and is not on any regular medications. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. On examination, the 2nd and 3rd distal interphalangeal joints (DIPs) and both hands are swollen and tender. Additionally, there is a fusiform swelling of the 2nd toe on his right foot. There are no nail changes and no rashes. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition disease (CPPD)
explanation:
Psoriatic arthritis
Inflammatory arthritis involving DIP swelling and dactylitis points to a diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis. Psoriatic arthritis is the correct answer. He has clinical features of inflammatory arthritis in the form of inflammatory joint pain and clinical evidence of synovitis. Furthermore, the fusiform swelling of one of his toes is likely to reflect dactylitis in this context. The most likely diagnosis is, therefore, psoriatic arthritis, which is often characterised by DIP-predominant arthritis and dactylitis.

Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition disease (CPPD)
CPPD is incorrect. This does not typically affect the DIP joints. If it presents as a small joint polyarthritis, it typically affects the wrists and metacarpophalangeal joints.

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis (OA) is incorrect. The patient describes inflammatory joint pain rather than mechanical sounding pain, which would be worse, rather than better, with activity. Additionally, dactylitis is not a feature of OA.

Reactive arthritis
Reactive arthritis is incorrect. This is an HLA-B27 associated disease like psoriatic arthritis. It can cause dactylitis. However, it tends to cause arthritis that predominantly affects the lower limbs. Furthermore, there is no history in this scenario of preceding infection or other typical features of this condition such as conjunctivitis or urethritis. Therefore, it is a less likely diagnosis.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. This does not typically affect the DIP joints. It is a small joint polyarthritis affecting the metacarpophalangeal joints and proximal interphalangeal joints if it affects the hands.

stem: A 52-male presented with intermitted fever, malaise, and arthralgia in his knees and hands. These symptoms had been on-going for the last 8 weeks. He has also noted frank haematuria on 5 occasions over the last week and a mottled lace-like discolouration of his skin on both his legs. Observation and blood tests are as follows: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg Heart rate 86 bpm Temperature 37.8 deg C Respiratory rate 12 /min oxygen saturation 96 % Hb 136 g/L Male: (135-180) Platelets 398 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 10 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Urea 7.8 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 150 µmol/L (55 - 120) CRP 50 mg/L (< 5) HBsAg positive Anti-HBs negative Anti-HBc positive p-ANCA positive c-ANCA negative What neurological disorder is associated with the most likely diagnosis?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
explanation:
Mononeuritis multiplex
Polyarteritis nodosa can cause a mononeuritis multiplex syndrome. The patient's symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgia, frank haematuria, livedo reticularis (mottled lace-like discolouration of skin), raised inflammatory markers, poor renal function, positive hepatitis B serology, and positive perinuclear-antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (p-ANCA) point to a diagnosis of polyarthritis nodosa (PAN). PAN is a vasculitis affecting medium-sized arteries with necrotizing inflammation leading to aneurysm formation. PAN is more common in middle-aged men and is associated with mononeuritis multiplex and sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Mononeuritis multiplex is a painful, asymmetrical, asynchronous sensory and motor peripheral neuropathy involving isolated damage to at least 2 separate nerve areas. Multiple nerves in random areas of the body can be affected.

Amyotrophy
Amyotrophy is a nerve disorder that is a complication of diabetes mellitus. It affects the thighs, hips, buttocks and legs, causing pain and muscle wasting.

Lambert-Eaton syndrome
Lambert-Eaton syndrome is an autoimmune disorder characterized by muscle weakness of the limbs. Around 60% of those with Lambert-Eaton syndrome have an underlying malignancy, most commonly small-cell lung cancer. Antibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels decrease the amount of calcium that can enter the presynaptic nerve ending, resulting in less acetylcholine being released from the neuromuscular junction which causes muscle weakness. In contrast to myasthenia gravis, the muscle weakness will improve with activity.

Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord is characterized by degeneration of the dorsal columns and the lateral columns of the spinal cord due to demyelination. It is a neurological complication of vitamin B12 deficiency. It commonly presents with sensory deficits (loss of proprioception and vibration sense), paraesthesia, weakness, ataxia, and gait disturbance.

Syringomyelia
Syringomyelia ('syrinx' for short) is a collection of cerebrospinal fluid within the spinal canal. The classical presentation is a loss of temperature and pain sensation in a cape-like distribution (neck and arms), but preservation of light touch, proprioception and vibration. This is due to the crossing spinothalamic tracts in the anterior commissure of the spinal cord being the first tracts to be affected. Other symptoms and signs include spastic weakness (predominantly of the upper limbs), paraesthesia, neuropathic pain, and upgoing plantar reflexes, as well as bowel and bladder dysfunction.

stem: A 74-year-old woman attends the clinic with a 12-month history of widespread bone pain and lower limb weakness. On examination, you note grade 4 weakness of the proximal lower limb muscles. Blood results are as follows: Calcium 2.05 mmol/L (2.1-2.6) Phosphate 0.6 mmol/L (0.8-1.4) PTH 21.2 pmol/L (1.6 - 6.9) ALP 260 u/L (30 - 100) What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Osteomalacia
Low serum calcium, low serum phosphate, raised ALP and raised PTH - osteomalacia. The clinical features (widespread bone pain and proximal myopathy), and laboratory features (low serum calcium, low serum phosphate, raised ALP and raised PTH) are classic of this disorder.

Osteopenia
Osteopenia and Osteoporosis are incorrect. These are quantitative, not qualitative, disorders of bone mineralisation. Laboratory bone profile results are usually normal, and the diagnosis relies on a DEXA scan.

Osteoporosis
Osteopenia and Osteoporosis are incorrect. These are quantitative, not qualitative, disorders of bone mineralisation. Laboratory bone profile results are usually normal, and the diagnosis relies on a DEXA scan.

Primary hyperparathyroidism
Primary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. This condition is characterised by hypercalcemia with a raised or inappropriately normal PTH.

Rickets
Rickets has a similar disease process to osteomalacia (e.g. disorder of impaired mineralisation of the osteoid) however this disease occurs in growing children. It causes bone pain, poor growth and soft, weak bones that can lead to bone deformities.

stem: A 33-year-old man who is suspected of having ankylosing spondylitis has a lumbar spine x-ray. Which one of the following features is most likely to be present?
explanation:
Sclerosis
In ankylosing spondylitis, the lumbar spine x-ray often shows sclerosis of the sacroiliac joints. This is due to chronic inflammation leading to new bone formation and fusion of the joint, which appears as increased density or sclerosis on x-ray.

Wedge shaped discs
Wedge-shaped discs are more indicative of osteoporosis or vertebral compression fractures, not ankylosing spondylitis. In these conditions, the vertebral bodies may collapse, leading to a wedge shape.

'Rugger-Jersey' spine
'Rugger-Jersey' spine refers to the appearance of increased density at the upper and lower ends of the vertebral bodies, giving them a striped appearance similar to a rugby jersey. This is typically seen in hyperparathyroidism.

Osteophytes
Osteophytes are bony outgrowths that form along joint margins. They usually develop as part of the body's response to ongoing inflammation in arthritis, particularly osteoarthritis - not ankylosing spondylitis.

Subchondral cysts
Subchondral cysts are not a common feature in ankylosing spondylitis. Subchondral cysts are fluid-filled sacs that can form in joints affected by osteoarthritis and other degenerative joint diseases due to wear and tear on the cartilage and underlying bone.

stem: A 22-year-old gymnast reports pain in the lateral forearm that is worse on straightening the wrist or fingers. She also sometimes feels an unusual sensation in her hand a bit like pins and needles. On examination, she is tender distal to the common extensor origin with no pain overlying the lateral epicondyle itself. What is the most likely cause of her forearm pain?
explanation:
Radial tunnel syndrome
Radial tunnel syndrome presents similarly to lateral epicondylitis however pain is typically distal to the epicondyle and worse on elbow extension/forearm pronation. Radial tunnel syndrome can be difficult to distinguish from lateral epicondylitis as both conditions present with lateral elbow pain. Radial tunnel syndrome however typically presents with tenderness distal to the common extensor origin in comparison to lateral epicondylitis where there is pain over the common extensor origin. It is most common in gymnasts, racquet players and golfers who frequently hyperextend at the wrist or carry out frequent supination/pronation. Patients can also complain of hand paraesthesia or aching at the wrist.

Lateral epicondylitis
Lateral epicondylitis typically presents with pain over the common extensor origin, not distal to it.

Cubital tunnel syndrome
Cubital tunnel syndrome patients experience tingling and numbness in the 4th and 5th finger.

Olecranon bursitis
In olecranon bursitis, there would be presence of swelling over the posterior elbow.

Cervical radiculopathy
Cervical radiculopathy would cause a burning pain radiating from shoulder to fingers. There may be reduced cervical range of motion or pain as clues in the history.

stem: A 45-year-old office worker presents to the orthopaedic outpatient clinic with a 6-week history of unilateral heel pain. The pain is most severe when getting out of bed in the morning and after prolonged sitting. On examination, there is tenderness over the medial aspect of the calcaneus. The pain improves with walking but worsens again after rest. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Plantar fasciitis
Plantar fasciitis is the correct answer and represents the most common cause of heel pain in adults. The clinical presentation is classic for this condition: medial calcaneal tenderness, pain that is worst with the first steps in the morning or after periods of rest, and improvement with initial walking before worsening again. This pattern occurs because the plantar fascia tightens during rest and stretches painfully when weightbearing resumes. The medial calcaneal tuberosity is the typical site of maximum tenderness as this is where the plantar fascia originates. The condition commonly affects middle-aged adults, particularly those with occupations involving prolonged standing or sitting. Management focuses on rest, appropriate footwear with good arch support, and the use of insoles or heel pads to reduce strain on the plantar fascia.

Calcaneal stress fracture
Calcaneal stress fracture would typically present with more constant, severe pain that worsens progressively with weight-bearing activity rather than improving initially with walking. The pain pattern would be different, usually becoming worse throughout the day with activity rather than showing the characteristic morning stiffness and post-rest exacerbation seen in this case.

Achilles tendinopathy
Achilles tendinopathy causes pain and tenderness along the Achilles tendon, typically 2-6cm above its insertion into the posterior calcaneus. The pain location would be posterior rather than medial, and the characteristic morning stiffness pattern of plantar fasciitis would not be expected.

Tarsal tunnel syndrome
Tarsal tunnel syndrome involves compression of the posterior tibial nerve and typically causes burning, tingling, or numbness along the medial foot and toes, often with nocturnal symptoms. While it can cause medial heel discomfort, the neurological symptoms and different pain character would distinguish it from this presentation.

Calcaneal bursitis
Calcaneal bursitis involves inflammation of the bursa between the Achilles tendon and calcaneus, causing posterior heel pain rather than the medial tenderness described. The pain pattern would also differ from the characteristic rest-related exacerbation seen in plantar fasciitis.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to his general practitioner complaining of cold hands and skin colour changes. He works as a gold miner and has recently arrived in the UK from Ghana. On examination, his hands were cool to touch, and his fingertips were pale. There was no ulceration. There was no proximal muscle weakness or tenderness. There is no rash or skin hardening. Blood tests: ANA negative ENA negative Creatine kinase 400 U/L (0-320) Given the likely diagnosis, what is the probable underlying cause?
explanation:
Occupational
Use of vibrating tools may result in Raynaud's phenomenon. Occupational is correct. The patient has cool hands and pale fingertips. In a patient from Ghana, this is likely to reflect Raynaud's phenomenon where the triphasic skin changes may be less apparent. Gold miners may develop hand-arm vibration syndrome and secondary Raynaud's phenomenon from the use of vibrating tools.

Dermatomyositis
Dermatomyositis is incorrect. CK levels are often higher in people from an African background. The CK is only mildly elevated and there are no other clinical features to suggest dermatomyositis.

Sjogren's syndrome
Sjogren's syndrome is incorrect. There is no mention of Sicca symptoms, such as a dry mouth or dry eyes and the ANA and ENA are negative making this diagnosis unlikely.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus is incorrect. In the recent EULAR classification for SLE, a positive ANA at a dilution of at least 1:80 is a requirement for SLE.

Systemic sclerosis
Systemic sclerosis is incorrect. ANA negative scleroderma is rare. Additionally, there are no other cutaneous features to suggest the diagnosis.

stem: A 21-year-old man presents to the GP with several months of low back pain and stiffness. There is no history of trauma. He finds the symptoms worse upon waking and they gradually ease off, especially with exercise. Sitting for long periods of time seems to worsen the symptoms. The symptoms occasionally trouble him at night, for which he has to get up and mobilise to settle the pain again. On examination, there is reduced lateral flexion and reduced forward flexion. An x-ray of the spine is requested. Which of the following features on x-ray is most commonly seen with this condition?
explanation:
Syndesmophytes
Syndesmophytes (ossification of outer fibres of annulus fibrosus) are a feature of ankylosing spondylitis. The diagnosis here is that of ankylosing spondylitis, given the patient's age and symptoms. From the options listed above, the most classic finding is that of syndesmophytes. Whilst they are found in a few other conditions, they are most recognised as a feature of ankylosing spondylitis.

Apical lung fibrosis
Apical lung fibrosis may occur, leading to a restrictive defect on spirometry, along with the effects of kyphosis and ankylosis of the costovertebral joints. However, it is not as common a feature of ankylosing spondylitis on imaging as syndesmophytes.

Joint space narrowing
Joint space narrowing is incorrect - this is recognised as a later feature of ankylosing spondylitis, following initial joint space widening, but to a lesser extent than syndesmophytes. It is more recognised as a feature of osteoarthritis.

Bamboo spine
Bamboo spine, whilst a feature of ankylosing spondylitis, is a late sign and much more uncommon than syndesmophytes.

Subchondral sclerosis
Subchondral sclerosis is incorrect. Whilst this is seen in ankylosing spondylitis (to a lesser extent than syndesmophytes), it is more recognised as a feature of imaging in osteoarthritis.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is referred to rheumatology outpatients with a 4 month history of joint pains, myalgia and generalised lethargy. An autoantibody screen reveals she is ANA positive and antiribonucleoprotein positive. The creatine kinase is elevated at 525. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Mixed connective tissue disease
The most likely diagnosis for this patient is Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD). The presence of anti-ribonucleoprotein (anti-RNP) antibodies, along with the positive ANA result and the patient's symptoms of joint pains, myalgia, and generalised lethargy, are highly suggestive of MCTD. MCTD is a systemic autoimmune disease that presents with features of multiple connective tissue disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), scleroderma, and polymyositis.

Systemic lupus erythematous
The first incorrect option is Systemic lupus erythematous (SLE). Although the patient has a positive ANA result and some clinical features consistent with SLE, the presence of anti-RNP antibodies makes MCTD more likely. SLE typically presents with a variety of symptoms such as malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, arthritis, serositis, nephritis, neurologic manifestations or haematologic abnormalities.

Polymyositis
Polymyositis is another incorrect option. While the elevated creatine kinase level suggests muscle inflammation which could be seen in polymyositis, the presence of anti-RNP antibodies is not typical for this condition. Polymyositis usually presents with symmetrical proximal muscle weakness and may have associated interstitial lung disease or other extramuscular manifestations.

Dermatomyositis
Dermatomyositis, another incorrect choice, shares some clinical features with polymyositis but also includes characteristic skin findings such as Gottron's papules or heliotrope rash. However, similar to polymyositis, dermatomyositis does not typically present with anti-RNP antibodies.

CREST syndrome
Finally, CREST syndrome, part of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis spectrum rather than a distinct entity itself nowadays, is also an incorrect option. CREST stands for calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia. While some of these features can overlap with MCTD, the presence of anti-RNP antibodies makes MCTD more likely in this case.

stem: A 26-year-old man presents to his GP complaining of recurrent cramping at the very start of his weekly five-a-side football game. He is usually able to continue playing and the cramps always resolve after the first 10 minutes of play. After these games, his urine can sometimes have the appearance of 'coca-cola'. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
McArdle's syndrome
Repeated cramping, rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria after short bouts of exercise can point towards McArdle's disease. The time of onset, the 'second wind' phenomenon, and recurrent symptoms are suggestive of McArdle's syndrome.

stem: A 72-year-old female known to have osteoporosis is started on alendronate. Which one of the following side-effects is it most important to warn her about?
explanation:
Heartburn
Bisphosphonates can cause a variety of oesophageal problems. Whilst the development of any new problem following the introduction of a new drug warrants medical review, it is particularly important to warn patients starting bisphosphonates about symptoms which could suggest an oesophageal reaction, especially with alendronate.

stem: A 52-year-old man is reviewed in rheumatology clinic. He has rheumatoid arthritis and has tried a number of medications over the years, with very little success in reducing his symptoms. The rheumatologist decides to trial him on hydroxychloroquine. Which of the following adverse effects should the patient be warned about?
explanation:
Retinopathy
Hydroxychloroquine - may result in a severe and permanent retinopathy. The correct answer is hydroxychloroquine - a recognised side effect of this drug is 'bull's eye retinopathy', which may result in severe and permanent visual loss. Recent publications suggest that this is more common than previously thought, and the most recent guidelines from the Royal College of Ophthalmologists propose regular monitoring.

Cataracts
Cataracts are a recognised, relatively-common side effect of long-term steroid use, as is open-angle glaucoma.

Open-angle glaucoma

Scleritis
Scleritis and uveitis have been linked in case reports with bisphosphonates, although there is not much data beyond this. They are, however, linked to a number of rheumatological and inflammatory conditions.

stem: A 33-year-old female presents with pain and stiffness in her right knee, which she's had for the last 3 months. On further questioning, she also has pain and stiffness in her left wrist and the distal interphalangeal joint of her right index finger. Her symptoms are worse in the morning and seem to improve throughout the day. She reports that her late mother also had joint problems; but does not know the diagnosis, although she recalls that her fingers were completely swollen before she started treatment. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Psoriatic arthritis
Inflammatory arthritis involving DIP swelling and dactylitis points to a diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis. Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy, that most commonly presents as an oligoarthritis (usually involving fewer than 3 joints for the first 6 months). It can involve any joint in the body, but unlike rheumatoid arthritis often affects the distal interphalangeal joints. Other common symptoms of psoriatic arthritis include dactylitis 'sausage digit', inflammation of an entire digit and nail changes such as onycholysis. In 15-20% of cases, symptoms of arthritis are detected before psoriasis appears.

Gonococcal arthritis
Gonococcal arthritis is a single or multiple joint septic arthritis caused by disseminated gonococcal infection.

Reactive arthritis
Reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome), is inflammatory arthritis that develops in response to an infection. The classic triad of symptoms is inflammatory arthritis of large joints, inflammation of the eyes (conjunctivitis or uveitis), and urethritis/cervicitis. Reactive arthritis: conjunctivitis/uveitis, urethritis/cervicitis and arthritis 'can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree'.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis typically presents as a symmetrical polyarthritis.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease which has a wide range of clinical and laboratory features which can be remembered using the pneumonic 'SOAP BRAIN MD'. 'SOAP BRAIN MD' Serositis: pleurisy or pericarditis Oral ulcers Arthritis Photosensitivity Blood: anaemia, leukopenia, lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia Renal disorder: lupus nephritis - minimal mesangial, mesangial proliferative, focal, diffuse, membranous and advanced sclerosis Antinuclear antibody Immunology: anti-Smith, anti-ds DNA and antiphospholipid antibody Neurologic disorder: seizures or psychosis Malar rash Discoid rash.

stem: A 31-year-old female intolerant of methotrexate is started on azathioprine for rheumatoid arthritis. Routine blood monitoring shows: Hb 7.9 g/dl Plt 97 * 109/l WBC 2.7 * 109/l Which of the following factors will predispose her to azathioprine toxicity?
explanation:
Thiopurine methyltransferase deficiency
Azathioprine - check thiopurine methyltransferase deficiency (TPMT) before treatment Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) deficiency is present in about 1 in 200 people and predisposes to azathioprine related pancytopaenia.

stem: A 79-year-old man presents with a history of lower back pain and right hip pain. Blood tests reveal the following: Calcium 2.20 mmol/l Phosphate 0.8 mmol/l ALP 890 u/L What is the most likely diagnosis?

stem: A 66-year-old female is on long-term prednisolone therapy for polymyalgia rheumatica. What is the most appropriate protection against osteoporosis?
explanation:
Oral bisphosphonate
Oral bisphosphonate therapy is recommended for patients older than 65 years who have taken, or who are likely to remain on oral corticosteroids for more than 3 months.

stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding psoriatic arthropathy?

stem: A 47-year-old female is referred to the rheumatology clinic due to cold fingers. Which connective tissue disease is most strongly associated with Raynaud's phenomenon?
explanation:
Systemic sclerosis
Raynaud's phenomenon is associated with all the above conditions but is most strongly linked to systemic sclerosis. Around 2% of women and 6% of men with Raynaud's phenomenon develop systemic sclerosis.

stem: A 74-year-old man presents with a severe throbbing headache on the right side of his head. He has now had this pain for around 6-7 days but reports no obvious trigger. There have been no visual disturbances or episodes of limb weakness. Neurological examination is unremarkable. The right side of his head is tender to touch but he cannot remember falling. Given the likely diagnosis what is the most important initial step?
options: Arrange an urgent orbital x-ray for suspected blow-out fracture
Arrange an urgent temporal artery biopsy
explanation:
Give high-dose oral prednisolone
This patient has temporal arteritis and requires high-dose oral steroids to prevent ocular complications.

stem: A 48-year-old female with left sided pins and needles in her left thumb, index and middle finger for several months, has been diagnosed with carpal tunnel syndrome. What features in her past medical history has predisposed her to the condition?

Obesity

High blood pressure

Muscle biopsy demonstrates elevated glycose concentration and

history of painful hands and fingers. Her past medical history includes
hypothyroidism for which she takes levothyroxine 125 micrograms/day
and a recent diagnosis of gastro-oesophageal reflux.
On examination, her observations are within normal limits. Her hands are
examined, as shown below:
© Image used on license from DermNet NZ

Anti-CCP antibody
Anti-Jo antibody
Anti-centromere antibody
Anti-nuclear antibody

Question 115 of 181
A 45-year-old woman presents to the rheumatology clinic with a 6-week
history of painful hands and fingers. Her past medical history includes
hypothyroidism for which she takes levothyroxine 125 micrograms/day
and a recent diagnosis of gastro-oesophageal reflux.
On examination, her observations are within normal limits. Her hands are
examined, as shown below:
© Image used on license from DermNet NZ
What investigation will most likely confirm the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Anti-centromere antibody is correct. This patient's finger is
erythematous with dry and tightened skin with evidence of digital
ulceration. The fingernails also appear fragile and brittle with ragged
cuticles. The examination findings combined with the history of painful
hands, and a recent diagnosis of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
consistent with systemic sclerosis. Systemic sclerosis (or scleroderma)
is an autoimmune connective tissue disease that is characterised by the
fibrosis of the skin and organs secondary to the overproduction of
collagen. Other symptoms include vasculopathy with Raynaud's
phenomenon. Multiple antibodies can be present in systemic sclerosis.
However, one of the more specific antibodies for systemic sclerosis is
the anti-centromere antibody that is most commonly associated with
limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.
Anti-CCP antibody is incorrect. Anti-CCP is associated with rheumatoid
arthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis can cause painful joints, particularly
smaller joints in a symmetrical distribution. Dermatological features are
less commonly seen and include rheumatoid nodules and erythema
nodosum. Rheumatoid arthritis does not explain this patient's
presentation.
Anti-Jo antibody is incorrect. This is positive in dermatomyositis which
is an autoimmune inflammatory disorder characterised by myopathy and
dermatological manifestations including skin lesions (e.g. heliotrope
rash, Gottron's papules and nail fold capillary dilatation). This is not what
is seen in this patient.
Anti-nuclear antibody is incorrect. Although ANA antibodies are present
in up to 90% of patients with systemic sclerosis, it is not a specific
finding as ANA antibodies are present in numerous inflammatory
conditions.
HLA-B27 testing is incorrect. This is present in numerous seronegative
spondyloarthropathies including ankylosing spondylitis and reactive
arthritis. However, neither condition gives rise to the skin changes seen
in this patient.

explanation:
This patient's blood results show pancytopenia with low haemoglobin,
platelets and white cell count. He is also experiencing symptoms of
anaemia with increasing lethargy and exertional shortness of breath.
When investigating a patient with symptomatic pancytopenia, it is
important to exclude any iatrogenic causes, such as medication. This
patient has recently been started on azathioprine, an
immunosuppressant medication. Of the drugs listed in this question,
azathioprine must not be given in conjunction with allopurinol as the 2
drugs cause an increased risk in haematological toxicity, such as that
seen in this patient.
Gliclazide is a sulfonylurea used in the treatment of diabetes mellitus.
The most important side effect to note is the risk of hypoglycaemia.
Lansoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor used in the treatment of gastro-
oesophageal reflux disease. Side effects include electrolyte imbalances
such as hypomagnesaemia and an increase in the risk of Clostridium
difficile infection.
Metformin is used in the treatment of diabetes mellitus. Gastrointestinal
side effects are the most common including diarrhoea and abdominal
pain. It does not interact with azathioprine.

side effects including pancreatitis, weight gain, alopecia and hepatic
toxicity. Rarely, it can cause agranulocytosis. However, it does not
interact with azathioprine and would not be contraindicated in this
patient.

explanation:
This patient has lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) given the history of
lateral elbow pain in a young sports player. The lateral epicondyle is an
attachment point for the extensors of the wrist joint. Therefore, pain on
resisted wrist extension is a diagnostic indicator.
Pain on resisted finger abduction tests the intrinsic hand muscles that
would not be implicated in lateral epicondylitis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is the correct diagnosis. Chronic kidney
disease (CKD) impairs phosphate excretion, causing
hyperphosphataemia, which binds calcium and lowers serum calcium
levels. Both hyperphosphataemia and low vitamin D (also occurs with
CKD) stimulate parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion, resulting in
elevated PTH (45 pmol/L). Elevated ALP reflects high bone turnover
from prolonged PTH activity. The patient’s CKD (urea 24 mmol/L,
creatinine 420 µmol/L) and electrolyte derangements (hypocalcaemia,
hyperphosphataemia) align with CKD-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-
MBD).
Adynamic bone disease arises from oversuppression of PTH, often due
to excessive calcium or vitamin D therapy. It features low/normal PTH
and normal/high calcium levels. The patient’s elevated PTH (45 pmol/L)
and hypocalcaemia (1.98 mmol/L) contradict this diagnosis. Elevated
ALP further supports active bone turnover, excluding adynamic disease.
Osteomalacia is caused by vitamin D deficiency or phosphate wasting,
leading to hypophosphataemia, hypocalcemia, and high PTH. This
patient has hyperphosphataemia (2.3 mmol/L), which reflects CKD-MBD,
not osteomalacia. In this case, the absence of vitamin D data does not
alter the conclusion, as phosphate retention and CKD dominate the
pathophysiology.
Osteoporosis is characterised by low bone density without mineral or
PTH abnormalities. This patient’s hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia,
and elevated PTH point to CKD-MBD rather than primary osteoporosis.
The lack of fragility fractures and the presence of CKD further exclude
this diagnosis.
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism involves autonomous PTH secretion after
prolonged secondary hyperparathyroidism, typically post-kidney
transplantation. It is characterised by hypercalcaemia due to unregulated
PTH release. This patient’s hypocalcaemia (1.98 mmol/L) and elevated
PTH exclude tertiary hyperparathyroidism.
Low serum calcium, raised serum phosphate, raised ALP and raised
PTH - chronic kidney disease leading to secondary
hyperparathyroidism

Continue treatment with alendronic acid with repeat DEXA scan in five years
explanation:
The patient's bone mineral density has improved secondary to her
treatment with alendronic acid. However, her recent back pain and
abnormal thoracolumbar x-ray suggest she has suffered from a
osteoporotic vertebral fracture. In one study, continuing alendronic acid
from five to ten years treatment reduced the incidence of clinical
vertebral fractures in all patients regardless of T score. Therefore,
continuing alendronic acid treatment would be recommended for this
patient.
Due to increased awareness of the potential complications of long-term
bisphosphonate treatment, treatment breaks (or 'drug holidays') are now
employed for some patients. Specifically, a treatment break should be
considered for patients less than 75 years old, with femoral neck T score
> - 2.5, no history of osteoporotic vertebral fracture and deemed low risk
following assessment by WHO Fracture Risk Assessment Tool (FRAX)
and National Osteoporosis Guideline Group (NOGG) guidance. For such
a patient, treatment would typically be suspended for two years with
repeat DEXA scan at the end of that period, or sooner in the event of
fragility fracture.
Parenteral osteroporosis treatments such as zoledronic acid or
denosumab should be considered if patient is intolerant of oral
bisphosphonates or in the event of treatment failure (defined as two or
more fractures on treatment, or one fracture and a fall in bone mineral
density).
Paskins Z, Warburton L. Bisphosphonates beyond five years. BMJ
2016;352:i264.

any regular medications. She frequently goes on holiday to hot-weather
climates.
On examination, there are red plaques with adherent scales in the
concha of both ears.

Given the likely diagnosis, what is the appropriate treatment?
Intravenous belimumab
Oral hydroxychloroquine
Oral steroids

Question 5 of 181
A 34-year-old patient presents to her general practitioner complaining of
a rash in both ears. She has no past medical history. She does not take
any regular medications. She frequently goes on holiday to hot-weather
climates.
On examination, there are red plaques with adherent scales in the
concha of both ears.
A skin biopsy demonstrates an interface dermatitis.
Given the likely diagnosis, what is the appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Topical steroids is the right answer. The patient presents with an
erythematous rash with an adherent scale in both ears. This is a classic
location for discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) and is known as
'Schuster's sign' when it affects the conchal bowl of both ears. A biopsy
demonstrating interface dermatitis is typical. The first-line treatment of
discoid lupus is topical steroids.
Discoid lupus erythematous - topical steroids → oral
hydroxychloroquine
Intravenous belimumab is incorrect. This is indicated as add-on therapy
for those patients with systemic lupus erythematosus with severe
disease not responding to conventional therapy. It is particularly
indicated for those with active musculoskeletal and cutaneous (which
may involve DLE) disease. It is not indicated for isolated DLE as a first-
line therapy.
Oral hydroxychloroquine is incorrect. Topical steroids should be tried in
the first instance. If this strategy is ineffective then oral
hydroxychloroquine can be commenced. It should be noted that if
discoid lupus was a manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus
then hydroxychloroquine should be commenced. Discoid lupus
erythematosus can exist as an isolated skin disease with a negative
antinuclear antibody (i.e. not as part of SLE) and in this setting, topical
steroids alone are a reasonable first option.
Oral steroids is incorrect. Oral corticosteroids are associated with
significant toxicity with long-term use and therefore are reserved only for
severe or refractory cases.
Topical imiquimod is incorrect. This is an immunomodulator that is used
in the treatment of genital warts, superficial basal cell carcinomas, and
actinic keratoses. The description of this bilateral auricular conchal rash
is not typical of a basal cell carcinoma (BCC), which is usually described
as a lesion having pearly rolled edges. Actinic (solar) keratoses can
cause scaly red plaques although they are more typically yellow. They
tend to occur as a consequence of sun damage over time and 34 would
be quite a young age to develop this type of lesion.
Discoid lupus erythematosus
Discoid lupus erythematosus is a benign disorder generally seen in
younger females. It very rarely progresses to systemic lupus
erythematosus (in less than 5% of cases). Discoid lupus erythematosus

Denosumab
Denosumab is a relatively new treatment for osteoporosis. It is a human
monoclonal antibody that prevents the development of osteoclasts by
inhibiting RANKL. Remember that osteoblasts build bone, osteoclasts
eat bone. It is given as a subcutaneous injection, at a dose of 60mg,
every 6 months.
A larger dose of denosumab (120mg) may also be given every 4 weeks
for the prevention of skeletal-related events (i.e. pathological fractures)
in adults with bone metastases from solid tumours. For example, you
may have noticed some of your breast cancer patients have been
prescribed denosumab.
Where does it fit in the management of osteoporosis?
Oral bisphosphonates are still given first-line, with oral alendronate being
the first-line treatment. If alendronate is not tolerated then NICE
recommend using an alternative bisphosphonate - either risedronate or
etidronate. Following this the advice becomes more complicated with
the next-line medications only being started if certain T score and other
risk factor criteria being met. Raloxifene and strontium ranelate were
recommended as next-line drugs in the NICE criteria but following recent
safety concerns regarding strontium ranelate it is likely there will be an
increasing role for denosumab.
NICE published a technology appraisal looking at the role of denosumab
in 2010. A link is provided.

explanation:
The clinical presentation is of diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis with
a scleroderma renal crisis (SRC). SRC is characterised by malignant
hypertension and oligo-anuric acute renal failure. A renal biopsy is not
necessary to confirm the diagnosis of classical SRC.
Captopril is correct. ACE inhibitors (ACEi) are the mainstay of therapy in
SRC. Initiation of their use allowed for major increased survival rates of
SRC over the last decades. The treatment goal is to achieve blood
pressure control as soon as possible. Importantly, ACE inhibitors must
be continued even if renal function is deteriorating.
Dialysis is incorrect. Indications for dialysis include uraemic
encephalopathy, uraemic pericarditis, uraemic haemorrhage, oliguria
resulting in clinically significant volume overload and respiratory distress
(that is refractory to medical management), metabolic acidosis due to
renal failure, and hyperkalaemia (>6.0) refractory to medical
management. The patient does not fulfil any of these criteria at the
current time.
Losartan is incorrect. Angiotensin II receptor blockade (ATII) may be
useful but is anecdotally less effective than ACE inhibitors, although
clinical experience with these agents has been limited.
Prostacyclin is incorrect. Continuous low doses of prostacyclin may be
added to standard therapy although there is no evidence that it improves
short-term and long-term prognosis.
Renal complications of systemic sclerosis - ACE-inhibitors
(preferably captopril)
Steroids and mycophenolate is incorrect. Steroids have been shown to
precipitate and worsen SRC. Clinical trials have yet to demonstrate the
efficacy of immunosuppressive agents for the treatment of SRC.

An 80-year-old retired GP with no past medical history presents to the

presumed chest infection in the last 3 months. In the last 2 days she has
been struggling to cope at home and has had two falls.
Blood tests show :
Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 60 mm/hour g/l
Creatinine Kinase 8000 U/L
Which of the following investigations would be LEAST helpful in the
workup?
explanation:
This lady seems to have polymyositis. An autoimmune profile is useful
as ANA is positive in one-third of patients. Anti-jo antibodies are positive
in 20% of patients and indicate a poorer prognosis with interstitial lung
disease. A full blood count may show leukocytosis or thrombocytosis.
AST/ALT are both muscle enzymes that will be elevated. Creatinine
kinase will also be elevated along with urine myoglobin. In some cases,
the patient may develop renal impairment from rhabdomyolysis and thus
U+Es should be monitored. A renal biopsy would not be diagnostically
helpful in this situation.

Prednisolone is correct. Steroids are the cornerstone of treatment for

Co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin is incorrect. This combination of

The radiological appearances, in this case, are more suggestive of
pneumonitis rather than pneumonia.
Co-trimoxazole is incorrect. This drug can be used to treat
pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) which is a serious infection caused by
the fungus Pneumocystis jirovecii. Although the patient is on low-dose
methotrexate, this is not particularly immunosuppressive, making PCP a
less likely diagnosis.

to co-trimoxazole can be used for severe cases of PCP characterised by
a PaO2 < 8 kPa.
Prednisolone and folinic acid is incorrect. The clinical and radiological
features are in keeping with methotrexate pneumonitis which should be
managed with high-dose steroids. Indications for folinic acid include
bone marrow toxicity which is not present in this case.

fine crackles while on methotrexate. This, combined with the presence of
infiltrates on chest x-ray, should raise the suspicion of methotrexate
pneumonitis.
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (Farmer's lung) would not be an
unreasonable differential diagnosis. However, in acute farmer's lung
patients would however present with a short history of fevers, chills,
malaise, headache and myalgia alongside breathlessness and dry
cough.
Interstitial lung disease would present with a longer history of
breathlessness and without fever or infiltrates on chest x-ray. They may
also have finger clubbing on examination.
Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia would be unusual without significant
immunocompromise, such as infection with untreated HIV. It would
however present with fever, exertional dyspnoea and dry cough and fine
interstitial changes on chest x-ray. Given there is no history of significant
immunocompromise, this is less likely than methotrexate-induced
pneumonitis.
Viral pneumonitis such as COVID-19 infection is also not an
unreasonable differential given the chest x-ray changes but it would be
unusual to have a 6-week history and there is no significant upper
respiratory tract symptoms or systemic features of rigors or myalgia
which you might expect with a viral illness.
Methotrexate may cause pneumonitis - typically presents with
cough, dyspnoea and fever

of Polymyositis. All of the options provided above are useful in the
diagnosis of polymyositis, which makes this question slightly tricky. Anti-
Jo-1 antibodies are characteristically associated with polymyositis and
indeed they are likely to point us to the right direction; however given the
fact that it is an Anti-nuclear antibody subtype it can be raised in other
systemic inflammatory condition such as Systemic Lupus

Electromyography can be used to distinguish between myopathic and
neuropathic causes of weakness and isolate the muscle group involved;
however it is fairly non-specific. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is
nowadays commonly employed, having the benefit of being non-invasive
and able to display large muscle groups, it has a high sensitivity however
it's non specific and cannot necessarily differentiate the changes of
inflammatory myopathy. Ultrasound of muscles has now been
surpassed by the use of MRI; this leaves us with muscle biopsy. Even
though it is less commonly used today due to its invasive nature and
difficulty in accessing the appropriate muscle group, it remains the most
sensitive and specific test in identifying polymyositis histopathologically,
provided that the right area of muscle is biopsied.

A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department with
worsening neck pain, which limits his participation in contact sports. He
is generally well otherwise and does not take any regular medications.
He smokes ten cigarettes daily and drinks alcohol occasionally.
The plain film radiograph of his C-spine showed:
© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
What is the next best step in his management?
explanation:
The neck radiograph shows syndesmophytes, squaring of the vertebrae
and bamboo spine, characteristic of ankylosing spondylitis.
Commence regular naproxen is the correct answer. NSAIDs are the first-
line treatment for ankylosing spondylitis. Therefore the patient should be
started on oral NSAIDs first.
Commence etanercept is incorrect. The 2010 European Alliance of
Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) guidelines suggest: 'anti-TNF
therapy should be given to patients with persistently high disease
activity despite conventional treatments'.
Commence sulfasalazine is incorrect. Disease-modifying drugs used to
treat rheumatoid arthritis (such as sulphasalazine) are only useful in
ankylosing spondylitis if peripheral joint involvement exists.
Limit physical exercise is incorrect. Physiotherapy and regular exercise
are recommended treatments for ankylosing spondylitis as per the
EULAR guidelines.
Urgent referral to spine surgery is incorrect. The most common surgical
procedure for ankylosing spondylitis is a laminectomy to relieve pressure
on the nerve roots. However, as this patient has no features of nerve root
compression, medical therapy is the next best step in his management.

hyperferritinaemia and negative testing for (antinuclear antibody) ANA
and rheumatoid factor. She has no life-threatening organ dysfunction
and therefore the initial management is with non-steroidal anti-
inflammatory medications.
NSAIDs are the first line treatment for Still's disease, not steroids
disease manifestations and organ dysfunction.
Methotrexate is incorrect. If the patient needs maintenance disease-
modifying therapy, then this would be an option. However, it is not used
to induce remission.
Antibiotics are incorrect. While the patient has a fever and raised
inflammatory markers, the clinical picture is that of Still's disease, rather
than infection.
Anakinra is incorrect. This is an interleukin (IL)-1 inhibitor used in the
treatment of a variety of inflammatory conditions including Still's
disease. It is used for severe cases that are refractory to initial
treatment.

typically hip and shoulder pain, with fatigue and raised inflammatory
markers. You would not expect to have a raised CK.

she went outside and turned a 'funny colour'. When she came back
inside her hands were very painful as they began to warm up. She had
managed in the past by wearing gloves outside but now had ulcers on
her fingertips which she had never experienced before. She also
complained of epigastric pain and had longstanding shortness of breath.
Her past medical history included pulmonary fibrosis and hypertension.
Her medications included propranolol, amlodipine, simvastatin and
omeprazole.
On examination the skin over her hands was dry and shiny and there was
severe digital ulceration on three fingertips of the left hand. There was
no exudate or erythema. The fingertips were dusky in colour and
extremely tender. The skin over the upper arms and chest appeared
normal. On auscultation of the lungs there were fine bibasal inspiratory
crepitations which did not alter in character upon coughing. Heart
sounds were normal with no added murmurs. There was a left
ventricular heave
Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan for this
lady?
Start flucloxacillin and stop all anti-hypertensive medications
Educate this lady about the use of gloves and hand-warmers and
increase her amlodipine dose

assessment
Stop propranolol and admit for an iloprost infusion

crepitations which did not alter in character upon coughing. Heart
sounds were normal with no added murmurs. There was a left

Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan for this

options: Start flucloxacillin and stop all anti-hypertensive medications
Educate this lady about the use of gloves and hand-warmers and increase her amlodipine dose
Stop amlodipine and refer for an urgent dermatology assessment
Stop propranolol and admit for an iloprost infusion
explanation:
This patient has secondary Raynauds associated with an underlying
diagnosis of Limited Systemic Sclerosis. Her disease is 'limited' as
opposed to 'diffuse' as she does not have skin changes proximal to the
elbows. She clearly has systemic involvement with pulmonary fibrosis
and oesophageal dysmotility (she has epigastric pain and is taking
omeprazole). Other features that were not mentioned in the question but
may be present in such patients include telangiectasia, typically over
mucosal surfaces, a 'beak-like' nose and microstomia, calcinosis and
renal impairment.
Severe digital ulceration in such patients can be treated with infusion of
a prostacyclin analogue such as iloprost. Prompt treatment is required
to avoid gangrene and loss of digits. Drugs such as beta blockers and
the oral contraceptive pill can exacerbate Raynauds phenomenon by
causing vascular spasm and should therefore be avoided.
There is no indication for flucloxacillin if the ulcers are not infected.
Gloves and hand-warmers can be very helpful for patients with Raynauds
phenomenon. Calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine and
nifidepine cause vasodilation in peripheral arterioles are also used to
treat Raynauds phenomenon. However, if there is severe ulceration
admission for an iloprost infusion is required.
Raynaud's phenomenon
Epoprostenol (amongst other prostaglandins) can be used in the
treatment of Raynaud's phenomenon

is 112/70 mmHg, pulse is 75 beats per minute and regular. You confirm

Question 22 of 181
A 28-year-old woman presents to the gastroenterology clinic for review.
She has been diagnosed with coeliac disease some 2 years earlier, and
has been suffering from severe tiredness, muscle aches and proximal
weakness for the past few months. On examination her blood pressure
is 112/70 mmHg, pulse is 75 beats per minute and regular. You confirm
proximal muscle weakness.
Investigations
Ca
2.0 mmol/l
Alkaline phosphatase
275 IU/l
Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
explanation:
Coeliac disease is known to interfere with absorption of fat soluble
vitamins, including vitamin D, and the low calcium and elevated alkaline
phosphatase, coupled with symptoms of proximal myopathy fits with a
diagnosis of osteomalacia. Vitamin D levels are therefore the next
investigation of choice.
CK and muscle biopsy are indicated for possible inflammatory myositis,
and the limited proximal weakness seen here, coupled with low calcium
is much more consistent with osteomalacia. Parathyroid hormone may
be elevated, but this is secondary to low vitamin D and calcium.
Electromyography is most useful for assessment of motor neuropathy,
which doesn't fit with the painful proximal muscle weakness seen here.

This lady has an array of positive antibodies associated with
rheumatological conditions. It is important however here to pay attention
to the actual symptomatology displayed by the patient and her
presenting complaints. The gender, age and history lean towards the
diagnosis of a systemic autoimmune condition, with Systemic lupus
erythematosus appearing as the most plausible explanation, given her
examination findings. The fleeting joint swelling is common in SLE,
alongside the non-specific symptoms and the characteristic butterfly
rash. The possibility of palindromic rheumatoid arthritis could explain
this fleeting arthralgia but does not account for the rest of the signs
observed. Polymyalgia rheumatica would be rare in the patient's age and
would not exhibit the findings seen. Mixed Connective Tissue Disorder
possibility is raised by the presence of anti-RNP antibodies, but one
should bear in mind the absence of other overlap features and that anti-
RNP antibodies can be found in up to 40% of patients with SLE. Finally
Hyperthyroidism is purely a red herring, with patients commonly
presenting in primary care with a fixed belief based on prior experiences,
whilst actually the pathological process is different.

wrists, left 2nd metacarpal-phalangeal (MCP) joint and right knee; blood
in his urine and a new rash on his cheeks, which particularly bothers him.
He also complains of chest pain of non-specific nature, onset about one
week ago. On examination, you note bilateral swollen MCP joints, a
hyperpigmented, raised erythematous rash on both cheeks. Neurological
examination reveals a mild distal tremor at rest and activity, with bilateral
KayserFleischer rings. He was diagnosed with Wilsons disease aged 18
years old and has no other past medical history. He is currently a
research assistant and lives alone. His medications include ibuprofen as
required, penicillamine started on diagnosis 2 years ago and he states
he has been buying zinc supplements over the counter after reading in a
journal that it may be helpful for his condition. Urine dip demonstrates

A 20-year-old male presents with a 4-day history of joint pain in both his

in his urine and a new rash on his cheeks, which particularly bothers him.
He also complains of chest pain of non-specific nature, onset about one
week ago. On examination, you note bilateral swollen MCP joints, a
hyperpigmented, raised erythematous rash on both cheeks. Neurological
examination reveals a mild distal tremor at rest and activity, with bilateral
KayserFleischer rings. He was diagnosed with Wilsons disease aged 18
years old and has no other past medical history. He is currently a
research assistant and lives alone. His medications include ibuprofen as
required, penicillamine started on diagnosis 2 years ago and he states
he has been buying zinc supplements over the counter after reading in a
journal that it may be helpful for his condition. Urine dip demonstrates
3+ blood, 1+ protein, no leucocytes or nitrites. Which blood test is most
likely to be diagnostic of his most recent admission?
explanation:
The patient describes haematuria, a new erythematous rash on sun-
exposed regions and arthritis, on a background of previous penicillamine
use: this is consistent with drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DLE). A
number of medications are known to induce DLE, including
penicillamine, procainamide, minocycline, hydralazine and a number of
anti-epileptics. There is no specific diagnostic test for DLE: a
combination of a drug known to induce DLE, the presence of ANA and
resolution of symptoms on offending drug withdrawal. However, it is
known that anti-histone antibodies are particularly sensitive to DLE,
positive in up to 95% of DLE patients. Anti-C1q antibody can be present
but is particularly predictive of lupus nephritis later in the disease. Unlike
systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), anti-dsDNA is often not present in
DLE.
The patient's symptoms are not consistent with that of zinc poisoning,
classically presenting with abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea. The
treatment of Wilsons disease is initially involves a copper-chelating
agent, either penicillamine or trientene. Zinc is generally not used unless
the patient is intolerant of either. Liver transplantation is also considered
for those presenting in acute liver failure only.
Drug-induced lupus
In drug-induced lupus not all the typical features of systemic lupus
erythematosus are seen, with renal and nervous system involvement
being unusual. It usually resolves on stopping the drug.

Question 26 of 181
A 34-year-old man presents for review. He has been generally unwell
since an episode of diarrhoea four weeks ago, with joint pains, pain on
passing water and a rash on the soles of his feet:
What does this rash likely represent?
explanation:
The correct answer is keratoderma blennorrhagica. Keratoderma
blennorrhagica is a skin condition associated with reactive arthritis,
which is an autoimmune response to an infection in another part of the
body. The patient's history of diarrhoea, joint pains, and pain on passing
water suggests that he may have reactive arthritis. The rash on the soles
of his feet supports this diagnosis as keratoderma blennorrhagica
typically presents as brownish-red hyperkeratotic plaques on the soles
and occasionally palms.
Pompholyx is an incorrect answer because it presents as small,
intensely itchy vesicles on the fingers, palms, and soles. It does not
match the description or appearance of the rash seen in this case.
HIV-associated dermopathy is also incorrect because it usually presents
as a widespread pruritic rash involving multiple body sites rather than
being confined to the soles. Moreover, there are no other clinical features
mentioned in the case that would suggest HIV infection.
Plantar pustular psoriasis can be ruled out because although it affects
the soles of feet and can cause discomfort during walking, it typically
presents with pustules and scale formation which are not observed in
this case.
Finally, mosaic warts are an incorrect answer because they present as
grouped verrucae (warts) with a rough surface on weight-bearing areas
of the foot. These warts are caused by human papillomavirus (HPV)
infection and do not fit with the clinical picture described for this patient.

the classic 'pencil-in-cup' changes that are often seen with psoriatic

Psoriatic arthropathy
Psoriatic arthropathy is an inflammatory arthritis associated with
psoriasis and is classed as one of the seronegative
spondyloarthropathies. It correlates poorly with cutaneous psoriasis and
often precedes the development of skin lesions. Around 10-20% of
patients with skin lesions develop an arthropathy, with males and
females being equally affected.

A 50-year-old lady presented with a 2 month history of breathlessness
on exertion, increasing leg swelling and more recently a rash across her
face. She was found to be in congestive heart failure, acute kidney injury
and she was being treated with diuretics. Her echocardiogram showed
severe left ventricular dysfunction. A few days into her admission she
sustained a ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest, which was successfully
treated and the patient was started on amiodarone and betablocker. Her
blood tests following the cardiac arrest did not show any electrolyte
abnormalities. She also had a coronary angiogram which revealed
normal coronary arteries. Subsequently, she was diagnosed with
systemic lupus erythematosous and associated lupus myocarditis and
she started appropriate immunosuppressive treatment for lupus.
What would be the best management for her ventricular fibrillation
cardiac arrest?
Continue amiodarone indefinitely
Implantable cardioverter defibrillator immediately and stop
amiodarone
Continue amiodarone and medical treatment of lupus and
review progress in clinic to decide about implantable cardioverter
defibrillator
Implantable cardioverter defibrillator immediately and
amiodarone indefinitely
None of the above
Question 28 of 181
A 50-year-old lady presented with a 2 month history of breathlessness
on exertion, increasing leg swelling and more recently a rash across her
face. She was found to be in congestive heart failure, acute kidney injury
and she was being treated with diuretics. Her echocardiogram showed
severe left ventricular dysfunction. A few days into her admission she
sustained a ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest, which was successfully
treated and the patient was started on amiodarone and betablocker. Her
blood tests following the cardiac arrest did not show any electrolyte
abnormalities. She also had a coronary angiogram which revealed
normal coronary arteries. Subsequently, she was diagnosed with
systemic lupus erythematosous and associated lupus myocarditis and
she started appropriate immunosuppressive treatment for lupus.
What would be the best management for her ventricular fibrillation
cardiac arrest?
options: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator immediately and stop amiodarone
Continue amiodarone and medical treatment of lupus and review progress in clinic to decide about implantable cardioverter defibrillator
Implantable cardioverter defibrillator immediately and amiodarone indefinitely
explanation:
This question aims to raise awareness about some of the aspects of the
management of cardiac arrest survivors.
According to ACC/AHA/HRS 2008 guidelines, implantable cardioverter
defibrillator (ICD) is indicated in survivors of ventricular fibrillation
cardiac arrest after investigations to identify the cause of the arrest and
exclude any reversible causes. Electrolyte abnormalities are among the
usual reversible causes, but there is a variety of other reversible causes
as well.
This patient sustained a cardiac arrest and had evidence of severe left
ventricular systolic dysfunction. However, lupus myocarditis is a
potentially reversible condition and so medical management is
warranted before insertion of ICD. An ICD might be indicated in the near
future if the patients left ventricular function does not improve following
treatment of her underlying condition. This is something that can be
reviewed in clinic with a repeat echocardiogram.
Amiodarone has a multitude of side effects and it should be continued
indefinitely only if there is a justifiable reason to do so.
